Troubleshooting Q28 of 200
What causes the OOMKilled (exit code 137) status on a pod?
A) The pod requested more CPU than available
B) The pod image is corrupted
C) Someone ran kubectl delete pod --force
D) The container exceeded its memory limit. The Linux kernel's OOM (Out-Of-Memory) killer terminated the process with SIGKILL (128+9=137). Check kubectl describe pod for "OOMKilled" in the State section
✅ Correct Answer: D

Exit code 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL). The pod used more memory than its resources.limits.memory. Fix: increase the memory limit, or optimize the application (e.g., reduce Django worker memory, add swap awareness). The OOM killer starts with BestEffort QoS pods first, then Burstable, then Guaranteed.

📝 QoS Classes — Eviction Priority Under Memory Pressure
OOM Killer Eviction Order
  QoS CLASS          REQUEST vs LIMIT       EVICTION PRIORITY
  ─────────         ─────────────────       ─────────────────
  BestEffort        No requests/limits      1st to die 💀
                    (any excess usage)
  
  Burstable         requests < limits       2nd to die ⚠️
                    (pod using more than
                     its request)
  
  Guaranteed        requests = limits       LAST to die ✅
                    (for both CPU+Mem)
  
  For anihpj-db: Set requests.memory = limits.memory
  → Guaranteed QoS → Protected from OOM eviction!
Troubleshooting Q29 of 200
Where are container logs stored on a Kubernetes worker node?
A) Inside the container at /var/log/app.log — that's the only location
B) On the node at /var/log/containers/ and /var/log/pods/. The kubelet symlinks container stdout/stderr to these directories using the container runtime's log driver
C) In etcd as part of the pod's state
D) In a cloud logging service — Kubernetes doesn't store logs locally
✅ Correct Answer: B

The full path: /var/log/containers/<pod>_<namespace>_<container>.log → symlink → /var/log/pods/<namespace>_<pod>/<container>/*.log. These are managed by the container runtime (containerd/Docker) and symlinked by kubelet for easy access.

📝 Container Log Path — Where Logs Live on the Node
Log File Path Structure
  /var/log/containers/
    anihpj-api-xxx_anihpj_web-<hash>.log  → symlink → 
  /var/log/pods/
    anihpj_anihpj-api-xxx/web/
      0.log    ← Container stdout (rotated: 0.log, 1.log, ...)
  
  # Direct access (on the node):
  tail -f /var/log/containers/anihpj-api-*.log
  
  # Cleanup old logs:
  find /var/log/containers -mtime +7 -delete
Troubleshooting Q30 of 200
You need to drain worker-1 for maintenance but DaemonSet pods (like the CNI plugin) are blocking the drain. What flag solves this?
A) --force
B) --delete-all-pods
C) --ignore-daemonsets — DaemonSet pods are managed separately and will be recreated on the node after uncordon
D) --skip-daemonsets-verification
✅ Correct Answer: C

DaemonSets place one pod per node. Draining a node means evicting pods — but DaemonSet pods would just be recreated immediately by the DaemonSet controller. --ignore-daemonsets skips them. Typical drain command: kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

📝 DaemonSet Drain — Why --ignore-daemonsets Is Needed
DaemonSet Pods Are Managed Differently
  kubectl drain worker-1
  ❌ Error: cannot delete DaemonSet pods (use --ignore-daemonsets)
  
  Why? DaemonSet controller recreates evicted pods immediately:
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Drain evicts calico-node-xxx  → DaemonSet recreates  │
  │   calico-node-yyy on worker-1 (infinite loop!)       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  # Correct drain command:
  kubectl drain worker-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
Troubleshooting Q31 of 200
What happens when containerd (the container runtime) on a worker node stops running?
A) The node eventually becomes NotReady. Existing pods continue running (processes stay alive) but no new pods can be created. kubelet reports the node as NotReady after the node-status-update-frequency timeout (default 5 min)
B) All pods immediately crash and the node is deleted from the cluster
C) Nothing — containers don't need a runtime once they're started
D) Kubernetes automatically installs Docker as a replacement
✅ Correct Answer: A

Running containers keep running (their processes are already forked). But kubelet can't create new pods, can't report container status, and eventually marks the node NotReady. Check: systemctl status containerd on the node, restart with systemctl restart containerd.

📝 Container Runtime Failure — Impact Assessment
What Stops When containerd Goes Down
  containerd stops:
  
  ✅ Existing containers KEEP RUNNING (processes already started)
  ❌ kubelet can't create NEW pods (ImagePullBackOff, CreateContainerError)
  ❌ kubelet can't report container status (node → NotReady after ~5min)
  ❌ kubectl exec/logs fail (need runtime to access containers)
  
  Fix: ssh worker-1 → systemctl restart containerd
  Check: systemctl status containerd | grep Active
Troubleshooting Q32 of 200
How do you find out WHY a pod was restarted?
A) kubectl logs <pod> --previous is the only way
B) Check the node's /var/log/messages file
C) Restart reasons are not tracked by Kubernetes
D) Use kubectl describe pod and look at the "Last State" section — it shows the reason (OOMKilled, Error, Completed) and exit code. Also check kubectl logs --previous to see the crashed container's logs
✅ Correct Answer: D

The "Last State" in kubectl describe pod is your restart forensics. It shows: Reason (OOMKilled/Error/Completed), Exit Code (137=SIGKILL, 1=app error, 0=normal), and timestamps. Combine with kubectl logs --previous to see what the container was doing right before it died.

📝 Pod Restart Forensics — Reading the Crime Scene
Decoding kubectl describe pod Output
  kubectl describe pod anihpj-api-xxx
  ...
  Last State:     Terminated
    Reason:       OOMKilled        ← Out of Memory!
    Exit Code:    137              ← 128 + 9 (SIGKILL)
    Started:      Wed, 04 Jun 10:00
    Finished:     Wed, 04 Jun 10:15  (ran 15 min)
  
  Exit Code Cheat Sheet:
  0   = Normal exit
  1   = Application error
  137 = SIGKILL (OOM or force delete)
  143 = SIGTERM (graceful shutdown)
  
  # See what the pod was doing before it died:
  kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx --previous --tail=50

2.2 Control Plane Component TroubleshootingQ33-Q44

Troubleshooting Q33 of 200
The kube-apiserver is not responding. Where do you find its logs?
A) kubectl logs -n kube-system pod/kube-apiserver
B) If running as a static pod: crictl logs <container-id> or check /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-*/. If running as a systemd service: journalctl -u kube-apiserver
C) The API server doesn't produce logs — only etcd does
D) Check the browser console when accessing the Kubernetes dashboard
✅ Correct Answer: B

In kubeadm clusters, the API server runs as a static pod (manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml). Since it's a pod, crictl logs works (kubeadm clusters use CRI, not Docker). You can also check /var/log/pods/ on the control plane node.

📝 Control Plane Log Locations — Quick Reference
Where to Find Logs for Each Component
  COMPONENT           LOG ACCESS METHOD
  ─────────           ─────────────────────────────────
  kube-apiserver      crictl logs $(crictl ps --name kube-apiserver -q)
                      OR /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-*/
  etcd                crictl logs $(crictl ps --name etcd -q)
  kube-controller-mgr crictl logs $(crictl ps --name kube-controller -q)
  kube-scheduler      crictl logs $(crictl ps --name kube-scheduler -q)
  
  # Alternative: check /var/log/pods/ on control plane node
  ls /var/log/pods/kube-system_kube-apiserver-*/
Troubleshooting Q34 of 200
What is etcd's role in Kubernetes, and what happens if etcd loses quorum?
A) etcd stores container images — if lost, pods can't start
B) etcd is a backup system — losing it has no impact on running pods
C) etcd is the distributed key-value store holding ALL cluster state (pods, services, configs, secrets). If quorum is lost (majority of etcd nodes unreachable), the cluster becomes READ-ONLY — no new resources can be created, modified, or deleted until quorum is restored
D) etcd only stores RBAC rules — everything else is in the kubelet
✅ Correct Answer: C

etcd uses RAFT consensus. Quorum = (N/2)+1 nodes. With 3 etcd nodes, you need 2 for quorum. If 2 fail, the remaining 1 can't elect a leader — cluster is read-only. All kubectl apply/create/delete fail. Running pods continue but no changes are possible.

📝 etcd RAFT Quorum — Why Odd Numbers Matter
Quorum = (N/2)+1 — Minimum Nodes for Consensus
  CLUSTER SIZE    QUORUM NEEDED    CAN TOLERATE FAILURE
  ────────────    ─────────────    ────────────────────
  1 node          1                0 (any failure = down)
  3 nodes         2                1 node failure
  5 nodes         3                2 node failures
  7 nodes         4                3 node failures
  
  With 3 etcd nodes, losing 2 = quorum lost = READ-ONLY cluster
  kubectl apply/create/delete all FAIL until quorum restored
Troubleshooting Q35 of 200
What is a static pod, and how does kubeadm use them?
A) A static pod is defined by a YAML file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. The kubelet watches this directory and manages these pods directly — they are NOT controlled by the API server, scheduler, or any controller. kubeadm uses static pods for all control plane components (apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager)
B) Static pods are pods that never restart
C) Static pods are created via kubectl but never deleted
D) Static pods are pods with fixed IP addresses
✅ Correct Answer: A

This is why control plane components appear as pods in kubectl get pods -n kube-system — the kubelet creates a mirror pod in the API server to represent each static pod. The name always ends with the node hostname (e.g., kube-apiserver-controlplane).

📝 Static Pods — How kubelet Manages Control Plane
Static Pod Lifecycle
  /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
    kube-apiserver.yaml      ← kubelet watches this directory
    etcd.yaml                ← Any YAML added here → pod created
    kube-controller-manager.yaml  ← YAML removed → pod deleted
    kube-scheduler.yaml
  
  kubelet creates "mirror pods" in API server:
  kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep controlplane
  kube-apiserver-controlplane     (mirror of static pod)
  
  To restart a control plane component:
  mv /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml /tmp/
  sleep 5
  mv /tmp/kube-scheduler.yaml /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
Troubleshooting Q36 of 200
How does the kube-scheduler decide which node to place a new pod on?
A) It picks the node with the lowest CPU usage
B) It randomly assigns pods to nodes in round-robin order
C) It asks etcd which node has the most free disk space
D) It uses a two-phase process: (1) FILTERING — eliminate nodes that can't run the pod (insufficient resources, taint mismatch, node selector mismatch), then (2) SCORING — rank remaining nodes by priority (least requested resources, pod affinity, topology spread)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Filtering (predicates): NodeHasSufficientCPU, NodeHasSufficientMemory, MatchNodeSelector, NoVolumeZoneConflict, ToleratesTaint. Scoring (priorities): LeastRequestedPriority, BalancedResourceAllocation, NodeAffinityPriority, InterPodAffinityPriority. Highest score wins.

📝 Scheduler — Filtering + Scoring Algorithm
How the Scheduler Picks a Node
  PHASE 1: FILTERING (Predicates) — Eliminate unfit nodes
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ NodeHasSufficientCPU    → Remove nodes without CPU     │
  │ NodeHasSufficientMemory → Remove nodes without RAM     │
  │ MatchNodeSelector       → Remove nodes without label   │
  │ NoVolumeZoneConflict    → Remove wrong AZ              │
  │ ToleratesTaint          → Remove tainted nodes         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  PHASE 2: SCORING (Priorities) — Rank remaining nodes
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ LeastRequestedPriority  → Favor less-busy nodes        │
  │ BalancedAllocation      → Favor balanced CPU/Mem       │
  │ NodeAffinityPriority    → Favor matching affinities    │
  │ InterPodAffinityPriority → Favor pod affinity matches  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Highest score wins → Pod scheduled to that node!
Troubleshooting Q37 of 200
How do you check if Kubernetes certificates are about to expire?
A) openssl x509 -in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt -text
B) kubeadm certs check-expiration — shows all certificates and their expiry dates. Certificates typically expire after 1 year. Renew with kubeadm certs renew all
C) kubectl get certificates
D) Certificates never expire in Kubernetes — they auto-renew
✅ Correct Answer: B

Expired certificates = cluster down. The API server, kubelet, and etcd all use TLS certificates. After 1 year, they expire and components can't communicate. kubeadm certs check-expiration is your warning system. In Kubernetes 1.29+, kubeadm can auto-renew certificates before expiry.

📝 Certificate Management — Check & Renew
Certificate Expiration Commands
  # Check all certificate expirations:
  kubeadm certs check-expiration
  
  OUTPUT:
  CERTIFICATE                    EXPIRES                  RESIDUAL
  admin.conf                     Jun 04, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
  apiserver                      Jun 04, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
  apiserver-etcd-client          Jun 04, 2027 10:00 UTC   364d
  
  # Renew ALL certificates:
  kubeadm certs renew all
  
  # After renewal, restart control plane:
  # (kubelet auto-restarts static pods when it detects changes)
Troubleshooting Q38 of 200
What is the difference between kubectl get componentstatuses (or kubectl get cs) and checking control plane health directly?
A) There is no difference — they are the same command
B) componentstatuses checks worker nodes, not control plane
C) kubectl get cs is a legacy command that queries the API server's internal healthz endpoints. It may report "Unhealthy" even when components are fine (network partition between API server and component). Better: check pod status with kubectl get pods -n kube-system
D) componentstatuses requires root access — it's not available to regular users
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl get cs is deprecated and unreliable. It checks if the API server can reach the controller-manager and scheduler ports, but network issues can cause false negatives. The reliable way: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'apiserver|etcd|controller|scheduler'.

📝 Why kubectl get cs Is Deprecated
Reliable vs Unreliable Health Checks
  UNRELIABLE (deprecated):        RELIABLE:
  kubectl get cs                  kubectl get pods -n kube-system
  ────────────────                ──────────────────────────────
  Checks if API server can        Checks if control plane pods
  reach component ports           are actually RUNNING
  
  False negatives: scheduler      Pod-based check shows:
  port unreachable due to         NAME                 STATUS
  network config on loopback      etcd-controlplane     Running
      only, but scheduler works   kube-apiserver-...    Running
      fine.                       kube-scheduler-...    Running
Troubleshooting Q39 of 200
What does the kube-controller-manager do when it detects a ReplicaSet has fewer pods than desired?
A) It creates new pods to match the desired count — this is the RECONCILIATION LOOP: observe actual state, compare with desired state, take action to close the gap
B) It sends an email alert to the cluster administrator
C) It marks the ReplicaSet as "Failed" and stops managing it
D) It waits for manual intervention from an operator
✅ Correct Answer: A

The reconciliation loop is the heart of Kubernetes: every controller continuously watches its resources, compares actual vs desired state, and acts to close the gap. If you delete a pod belonging to a ReplicaSet, the controller-manager notices and creates a replacement. This is why Kubernetes is "self-healing."

📝 Reconciliation Loop — The Heart of Kubernetes
Observe → Diff → Act — Infinite Loop
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          RECONCILIATION LOOP              │
  │                                           │
  │  1. OBSERVE: Read current state from API │
  │     "ReplicaSet has 2 pods, wants 3"      │
  │                                           │
  │  2. DIFF: Compare desired vs actual      │
  │     "Missing 1 pod"                       │
  │                                           │
  │  3. ACT: Create missing pod               │
  │     "POST /api/v1/namespaces/.../pods"    │
  │                                           │
  │  → Go back to step 1 (infinite loop)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  This runs continuously for EVERY controller:
  Node controller, ReplicaSet controller, Endpoint controller...
Troubleshooting Q40 of 200
How do you check etcd cluster health?
A) kubectl get etcd -n kube-system
B) curl http://localhost:2379/health
C) etcd health is automatically monitored — no manual check possible
D) ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key endpoint health
✅ Correct Answer: D

etcd health check requires TLS certificates (etcd is encrypted). The command returns the health status of each etcd member and identifies the current leader. Also use etcdctl endpoint status for detailed info including raft index, revision, and storage size.

📝 etcd Health Check — With Certificates
etcdctl Commands for Health & Status
  ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl \
    --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
    --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
    --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
    --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
    endpoint health
  
  OUTPUT:
  https://127.0.0.1:2379 is healthy: successfully committed proposal
  
  # Member list:
  etcdctl member list
  # Leader check:
  etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
Troubleshooting Q41 of 200
What happens when you run kubeadm certs renew all?
A) All certificates are regenerated and Kubernetes automatically restarts
B) All certificates in /etc/kubernetes/pki/ are renewed (new expiry date). You must restart control plane components (kubelet restarts static pods automatically when it detects manifest changes)
C) It only renews the CA certificate — individual component certs must be renewed separately
D) It creates a backup of old certificates but doesn't create new ones
✅ Correct Answer: B

After renewing certs, kubelet detects the changed static pod manifests and restarts control plane components. You should also copy the new admin.conf to ~/.kube/config. For worker nodes: kubeadm certs renew on the control plane, then update kubelet.conf on workers.

📝 Certificate Renewal — Full Workflow
Post-Renewal Steps
  # 1. Renew all certs
  kubeadm certs renew all
  
  # 2. Update kubeconfig
  cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf ~/.kube/config
  
  # 3. Restart control plane (kubelet auto-restarts static pods)
  # Wait 30s for pods to restart
  
  # 4. Verify
  kubectl get nodes
  kubeadm certs check-expiration
  
  # 5. For worker nodes:
  kubeadm certs renew apiserver-kubelet-client
  # Then copy new kubelet.conf to each worker
Troubleshooting Q42 of 200
What is the certificate chain in a kubeadm cluster?
A) All components use the same certificate — there is no chain
B) Certificates are issued by an external CA like Let's Encrypt
C) Self-signed CA → Component certificates. The CA at /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt signs: apiserver.crt, apiserver-kubelet-client.crt, front-proxy-ca.crt (signs front-proxy-client.crt), and etcd/ca.crt (signs etcd server/client/peer certs)
D) All certificates are stored in etcd, not on disk
✅ Correct Answer: C

The CA is the root of trust. If ca.crt expires, ALL certificates become invalid simultaneously. The CA certificate expires after 10 years (longer than component certs at 1 year). All certificates live in /etc/kubernetes/pki/.

📝 Certificate Chain — kubeadm PKI Structure
TLS Certificate Hierarchy in kubeadm
  /etc/kubernetes/pki/
    ca.crt / ca.key                          ← Root CA (10yr expiry)
    │
    ├── apiserver.crt / apiserver.key         ← API server serving cert
    ├── apiserver-kubelet-client.crt/key      ← API → kubelet
    ├── apiserver-etcd-client.crt/key         ← API → etcd
    │
    ├── front-proxy-ca.crt/key               ← Front proxy CA
    │   └── front-proxy-client.crt/key        ← Front proxy client
    │
    └── etcd/
        ├── ca.crt / ca.key                   ← etcd CA
        ├── server.crt / server.key           ← etcd serving
        ├── peer.crt / peer.key               ← etcd peer-to-peer
        └── healthcheck-client.crt/key        ← etcd health checks
Troubleshooting Q43 of 200
What do the kube-apiserver flags --advertise-address and --etcd-servers control?
A) --advertise-address is the IP address the API server tells other components to use to reach it (used by kubelet, scheduler, controllers). --etcd-servers is the comma-separated list of etcd endpoints the API server connects to for storing cluster state
B) --advertise-address is used for Google Ads; --etcd-servers is for DNS
C) These flags control pod networking, not the API server
D) These flags are deprecated and ignored in modern Kubernetes
✅ Correct Answer: A

If --advertise-address is wrong, kubelets can't reach the API server — nodes show NotReady. If --etcd-servers is wrong, the API server has no persistent storage — kubectl apply/create silently fails. These are in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.

📝 API Server Flags — Key Configuration
Critical kube-apiserver Flags
  # Found in: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  spec:
    containers:
    - command:
      - kube-apiserver
      - --advertise-address=192.168.1.10     ← IP others use to reach API
      - --etcd-servers=https://127.0.0.1:2379 ← etcd endpoints
      - --service-cluster-ip-range=10.96.0.0/12 ← Service CIDR
      - --service-account-issuer=https://kubernetes.default.svc
      - --service-account-key-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/sa.pub
      - --client-ca-file=/etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt
Troubleshooting Q44 of 200
The kube-scheduler pod is CrashLoopBackOff. Looking at logs, you see "connection refused" to the API server. What is the cause?
A) The scheduler doesn't connect to the API server — it's standalone
B) The scheduler pod needs more memory
C) The node's disk is full
D) The scheduler's kubeconfig file (mounted from /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf) has the wrong API server address or the API server isn't running yet. Check: grep server /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf and verify the API server pod is Running
✅ Correct Answer: D

Control plane components use kubeconfig files to authenticate with the API server. If server: address in the kubeconfig is wrong, the component can't connect. This typically happens after changing the API server's IP without updating component kubeconfigs.

📝 Control Plane Kubeconfig — Connection Debug
Component Kubeconfig Files
  /etc/kubernetes/
    admin.conf            ← kubectl admin access
    scheduler.conf        ← kube-scheduler → API server
    controller-manager.conf ← controller-manager → API server
    kubelet.conf          ← kubelet → API server
  
  # Check where a component connects:
  grep server /etc/kubernetes/scheduler.conf
  # server: https://192.168.1.10:6443
  
  # If IP changed, update ALL kubeconfig files:
  sed -i 's/old-ip/new-ip/g' /etc/kubernetes/*.conf

2.3 Application & Resource MonitoringQ45-Q56

Troubleshooting Q45 of 200
What is the difference between resources.requests and resources.limits for a container?
A) requests is the maximum; limits is the minimum
B) Requests = MINIMUM guaranteed (scheduler uses this to find a node with enough resources). Limits = MAXIMUM allowed (container is throttled/killed if it exceeds). Requests ≤ Limits always
C) They are interchangeable — Kubernetes ignores the difference
D) requests is for CPU only; limits is for memory only
✅ Correct Answer: B

Requests = "I need at least this much" (used for scheduling). Limits = "I must not exceed this" (used for enforcement). CPU: throttled when exceeding limit. Memory: OOMKilled when exceeding limit. Setting only limits without requests is a common mistake — the scheduler can't make good placement decisions.

📝 Requests vs Limits — Visual Comparison
CPU/Memory: Requests (Guaranteed) vs Limits (Ceiling)
  CONTAINER: anihpj-api
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ resources:                                               │
  │   requests:         ← SCHEDULER uses this to find a node │
  │     cpu: 200m       ← "I need at least 200m CPU"        │
  │     memory: 256Mi   ← "I need at least 256Mi RAM"       │
  │                                                          │
  │   limits:           ← KUBELET enforces this ceiling      │
  │     cpu: 500m       ← "Don't let me exceed 500m CPU"    │
  │     memory: 512Mi   ← "Kill me if I exceed 512Mi RAM"   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  CPU:  throttled at limit (slows down, doesn't die)
  RAM:  OOMKilled at limit (process killed, pod restarts)
Troubleshooting Q46 of 200
What are the three QoS (Quality of Service) classes in Kubernetes?
A) Gold, Silver, Bronze
B) High, Medium, Low
C) Guaranteed (requests=limits for both CPU and memory), Burstable (requests < limits, or one resource has no limit), BestEffort (no requests or limits set at all)
D) Production, Staging, Development
✅ Correct Answer: C

QoS determines eviction priority under resource pressure: BestEffort pods are killed FIRST, then Burstable pods that exceed their request, then Guaranteed pods LAST. For anihpj-db: use Guaranteed QoS (request = limit) to protect the database from eviction.

📝 QoS Classes — Memory Pressure Eviction Order
OOM Killer Eviction Priority — Who Dies First
  PRIORITY    QoS CLASS       CONDITION                  ANIHPJ EXAMPLE
  ────────    ─────────       ─────────                  ──────────────
  1st (dies)  BestEffort      No requests/limits set     Unconfigured pod
  2nd         Burstable       requests < limits          anihpj-web (256Mi/512Mi)
  3rd         Burstable       Using > its request        anihpj-api (using 400Mi of 200Mi req)
  LAST        Guaranteed      requests = limits          anihpj-db (1Gi/1Gi)
              (protected!)    for both CPU + memory
  
  For anihpj-db: SET requests.memory = limits.memory to get Guaranteed QoS
Troubleshooting Q47 of 200
What is a liveness probe, and what happens when it fails?
A) "Is my app alive?" probe. If it fails (after failureThreshold consecutive failures), kubelet KILLS and RESTARTS the container. Use for detecting deadlocked/stuck processes that can't recover on their own
B) "Can my app serve traffic?" probe — removes pod from Service endpoints if failing
C) "Is my app done booting?" probe — gives slow apps extra time
D) A probe that checks if the node has enough disk space
✅ Correct Answer: A

Liveness = restart if stuck. Readiness = remove from Service if not ready. Startup = wait for slow boot. Common mistake: setting liveness probe too aggressive (low initialDelaySeconds) — the app gets killed before it finishes starting up.

📝 Probe Comparison — Liveness vs Readiness vs Startup
3 Types of Probes — When to Use Each
  PROBE       QUESTION                  FAILURE ACTION       USE CASE
  ─────       ────────                  ──────────────       ────────
  Liveness    "Is my app ALIVE?"        RESTART container    Deadlock detection
              (hung/deadlocked?)                              Memory leak crash
  ─────       ────────                  ──────────────       ────────
  Readiness   "Can my app serve?"       Remove from Service   DB not ready
              (DB connection OK?)       (NO restart!)         Cache warming
  ─────       ────────                  ──────────────       ────────
  Startup     "Is my app done booting?" Disables liveness/    Slow-starting app
              (needs extra time?)       readiness until OK    Django migration
  
  Common mistake: liveness probe too early → app killed before it starts!
Troubleshooting Q48 of 200
What is a readiness probe, and how does it differ from a liveness probe?
A) They are identical — different names for the same thing
B) Readiness kills the pod; liveness removes from Service
C) Readiness is for HTTP; liveness is for TCP
D) Readiness determines if the pod should receive TRAFFIC (removed from Service endpoints if failing, but NOT restarted). Liveness determines if the pod should be RESTARTED. A pod can fail readiness but still be alive (e.g., database connection not ready yet)
✅ Correct Answer: D

Key distinction: Liveness failure = RESTART. Readiness failure = STOP SENDING TRAFFIC (pod keeps running). For anihpj-api: if the database is temporarily unavailable, readiness fails (no traffic), but liveness stays healthy (pod keeps running — it'll recover when DB returns).

📝 Liveness vs Readiness — YAML Example
anihpj-api Probes Configuration
  spec:
    containers:
    - name: api
      livenessProbe:       ← "Restart if deadlocked"
        httpGet:
          path: /healthz
          port: 8000
        initialDelaySeconds: 30
        periodSeconds: 10
        failureThreshold: 3   ← 3 failures = restart
  
      readinessProbe:      ← "Stop traffic if not ready"
        httpGet:
          path: /ready
          port: 8000
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 5
        failureThreshold: 3   ← 3 failures = no traffic
  
  /healthz: always returns 200 (liveness)
  /ready:   returns 503 when DB connection fails (readiness)
Troubleshooting Q49 of 200
What is the purpose of a startup probe?
A) It checks if the cluster has started successfully
B) It protects slow-starting applications. While the startup probe is running, liveness and readiness probes are DISABLED. Once startup succeeds, liveness/readiness take over. This prevents slow apps from being killed by aggressive liveness probes
C) It runs before the container starts to validate the image
D) It's the same as a readiness probe with a different name
✅ Correct Answer: B

Without startup probe: Django app needs 60s to start, but liveness probe starts checking at 10s and kills it. With startup probe: give it 120s (failureThreshold × periodSeconds), liveness waits. For anihpj-api: set startup probe with failureThreshold=12, periodSeconds=10 (120s total).

📝 Startup Probe — Protecting Slow-Starting Apps
How Startup Probe Shields Django From Premature Liveness Kill
  WITHOUT startup probe:
  T=0s   Pod starts, Django begins booting (migrations, cache warm)
  T=10s  Liveness probe fires → Django still loading → FAIL
  T=20s  Liveness fires again → FAIL (failureThreshold=3)
  T=30s  Kubelet KILLS the pod! 💀  (Django was at 90% boot...)
  
  WITH startup probe:
  T=0s    Pod starts, startup probe begins
  T=60s   Startup probe finally succeeds (Django fully booted)
  T=60s   Liveness/Readiness probes NOW start running
  Django has 60s safe window to boot without being killed!
  
  startupProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /healthz
      port: 8000
    failureThreshold: 12     ← 12 attempts
    periodSeconds: 10        ← every 10s = 120s total window
Troubleshooting Q50 of 200
What are the three types of probes Kubernetes supports?
A) HTTP, HTTPS, FTP
B) GET, POST, PUT
C) httpGet (HTTP GET request — returns 2xx/3xx = healthy), tcpSocket (TCP connection successful = healthy), exec (run command inside container — exit code 0 = healthy)
D) ICMP, TCP, UDP
✅ Correct Answer: C

httpGet: best for web apps (check /health endpoint). tcpSocket: best for databases (check port 5432 is open). exec: most flexible (run any script). For anihpj-api: use httpGet on /health. For anihpj-db: use tcpSocket on port 5432.

📝 Probe Types — httpGet, tcpSocket, exec
Three Probe Mechanisms
  TYPE         HOW IT WORKS              BEST FOR           ANIHPJ EXAMPLE
  ────         ─────────────             ────────           ──────────────
  httpGet      HTTP GET to URL           Web apps           /health on Django
               (2xx/3xx = healthy)                          /ready on Gunicorn
  
  tcpSocket    TCP connection check      Databases          PostgreSQL :5432
               (conn success = healthy)                      Redis :6379
  
  exec         Run command in container  Custom checks      pg_isready
               (exit 0 = healthy)                           redis-cli ping
  
  httpGet YAML:
  livenessProbe:
    httpGet:
      path: /health
      port: 8000
      httpHeaders:
      - name: X-Custom-Header
        value: probe
Troubleshooting Q51 of 200
What do initialDelaySeconds, periodSeconds, timeoutSeconds, and failureThreshold control in a probe?
A) initialDelaySeconds: wait before first probe. periodSeconds: how often to probe. timeoutSeconds: probe timeout. failureThreshold: consecutive failures before action. Example: initialDelaySeconds=10, periodSeconds=5, failureThreshold=3 → first probe at 10s, then every 5s, pod killed/removed after 3 consecutive failures (earliest: 10+5+5=20s)
B) They control how many times a pod can restart before being evicted
C) They are network timeout settings for the CNI plugin
D) They control the pod's priority class
✅ Correct Answer: A

These 4 parameters give you fine-grained control. Conservative settings for production: initialDelaySeconds=30, periodSeconds=10, timeoutSeconds=5, failureThreshold=3. This gives the app 30s to start, then checks every 10s, and only acts after 3 failures (30s of confirmed unhealthiness).

📝 Probe Timing Parameters — Visual Timeline
How Probe Parameters Control Timing
  initialDelaySeconds: 10   ← Wait 10s BEFORE first probe
  periodSeconds: 5          ← Check every 5 seconds
  timeoutSeconds: 3         ← Each probe must respond within 3s
  failureThreshold: 3       ← Need 3 consecutive failures to act
  
  TIMELINE:
  T=0s    Pod starts
  T=10s   1st probe (initialDelaySeconds)
  T=15s   2nd probe (periodSeconds=5)
  T=20s   3rd probe
  T=20s   All 3 failed → ACTION (failureThreshold=3)
          Earliest action: 10 + 5 + 5 = 20 seconds after pod start
  
  Conservative production settings:
  initialDelaySeconds: 30, periodSeconds: 10
  timeoutSeconds: 5, failureThreshold: 3
  → Action after ~60s of confirmed failure
Troubleshooting Q52 of 200
How do you see the logs of a PREVIOUS (crashed) container instance?
A) kubectl logs <pod> --all
B) You can't — logs are lost when a container crashes
C) kubectl logs <pod> --since-crash
D) kubectl logs <pod> --previous — shows logs from the PREVIOUS container instance that crashed. Essential for debugging CrashLoopBackOff
✅ Correct Answer: D

When a container crashes and restarts, the current container's logs are fresh. --previous shows you what the OLD container was doing when it died. Also useful: --tail=100 (last 100 lines), --since=5m (last 5 minutes), --timestamps (show when each line was logged).

📝 kubectl logs Flags — Quick Reference
Essential kubectl logs Options
  kubectl logs <pod>                     # Current container logs
  kubectl logs <pod> --previous          # CRASHED container's logs!
  kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>     # Specific container in pod
  kubectl logs <pod> --tail=100          # Last 100 lines
  kubectl logs <pod> --since=5m          # Last 5 minutes
  kubectl logs <pod> --timestamps        # Show when each line was logged
  kubectl logs -f <pod>                  # Follow (like tail -f)
  kubectl logs --all-containers <pod>    # ALL containers in pod
  kubectl logs deploy/anihpj-api          # All pods in deployment
  kubectl logs -l app=anihpj              # All pods with label
Troubleshooting Q53 of 200
A pod has two containers: "web" and "sidecar". How do you get logs from the sidecar container?
A) kubectl logs <pod> --all-containers always shows both
B) kubectl logs <pod> -c sidecar — specify the container name with -c. Without -c, kubectl logs defaults to the first container only
C) kubectl logs sidecar-<pod>
D) Sidecar containers don't produce logs
✅ Correct Answer: B

Multi-container pods require -c <container-name>. Use --all-containers to see logs from ALL containers. For anihpj: kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -c web (Django) vs kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx -c nginx (sidecar).

📝 Multi-Container Pod — Logging Each Container
Container Names in anihpj Pods
  Pod: anihpj-web-abc123
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Container: web (Django + Gunicorn)         │
  │   kubectl logs anihpj-web-abc123 -c web    │
  │                                            │
  │ Container: nginx (reverse proxy sidecar)   │
  │   kubectl logs anihpj-web-abc123 -c nginx  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  # If you omit -c, kubectl logs defaults to FIRST container
  # Use --all-containers to see all at once
Troubleshooting Q54 of 200
What does kubectl describe pod show that kubectl get pod doesn't?
A) They show the same information in different formats
B) Only the pod's IP address
C) Events (what happened to this pod chronologically), Conditions (PodScheduled, Initialized, ContainersReady, Ready), container states with reasons (ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled), volumes mounted, QoS class, tolerations, and node assignment
D) The pod's YAML definition only
✅ Correct Answer: C

kubectl describe is the #1 troubleshooting command. The Events section at the bottom is your timeline: "Failed to pull image", "Started container", "Liveness probe failed". For anihpj debugging: always start with kubectl describe pod before looking at logs.

📝 kubectl describe pod — The #1 Debugging Tool
What kubectl describe pod Reveals
  kubectl describe pod anihpj-api-xxx
  
  SECTIONS TO CHECK:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Conditions:          PodScheduled, Ready status          │
  │ Containers:          State (Running/Waiting/Terminated)  │
  │   State.Reason:      CrashLoopBackOff, OOMKilled, etc.  │
  │   Last State:        Previous crash reason               │
  │ Events:              CHRONOLOGICAL log of everything    │
  │   "Pulling image"    → "Started container"               │
  │   "Liveness probe    → "Killing container"               │
  │    failed"                                              │
  │ Volumes:             Mounted volumes & PVCs              │
  │ QoS Class:           Guaranteed/Burstable/BestEffort    │
  │ Tolerations:         Which taints are tolerated          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Troubleshooting Q55 of 200
How does metrics-server collect pod and node metrics?
A) It calls the kubelet Summary API on each node (https://<node>:10250/stats/summary) every 15 seconds, aggregates the data, and serves it via the metrics.k8s.io API. It does NOT store historical data — only the latest snapshot
B) It reads from Prometheus which scrapes container metrics
C) It runs inside each pod and reports metrics directly
D) It queries the cloud provider's monitoring API
✅ Correct Answer: A

metrics-server is lightweight by design — no persistent storage, no historical data. For long-term metrics, use Prometheus. The HPA relies on metrics-server for CPU/memory-based autoscaling. If metrics-server is down, kubectl top and HPA both stop working.

📝 metrics-server Architecture — Data Flow
How kubectl top Gets Metrics
  kubectl top pod
       │
       ▼
  API Server (apis/metics.k8s.io/v1beta1)
       │
       ▼
  metrics-server (kube-system deployment)
       │  scrapes every 15s
       ▼
  Kubelet Summary API (node:10250/stats/summary)
       │
       ▼
  cAdvisor (built into kubelet) → container CPU/Mem stats
  
  # Verify metrics-server is working:
  kubectl get --raw /apis/metrics.k8s.io/v1beta1/nodes
Troubleshooting Q56 of 200
The Events section of kubectl describe pod shows "Warning: FailedScheduling — 0/3 nodes are available." What does this mean?
A) All 3 nodes are down — the cluster is unavailable
B) The pod spec is invalid and can never be scheduled
C) The scheduler crashed and needs to be restarted
D) None of the 3 nodes can satisfy this pod's requirements. Possible reasons: insufficient CPU/memory, nodeSelector/affinity doesn't match any node, taints without tolerations, or node ports already in use. The message usually includes WHY each node was rejected
✅ Correct Answer: D

The full message usually says something like: "0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had taint {dedicated: database}, 2 Insufficient cpu." This tells you exactly what to fix. For anihpj: if you taint a node for database use but forget the toleration, the API pod gets this error.

📝 Scheduling Failure — Decoding the Error Message
"0/3 nodes are available" — Understanding Why
  kubectl describe pod anihpj-api-xxx | grep -A10 Events
  
  Events:
    Warning  FailedScheduling  0/3 nodes are available:
      1 node(s) had taint {dedicated: database}  ← Tainted!
      2 Insufficient cpu                          ← No CPU!
  
  FIX OPTIONS:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. Remove taint: kubectl taint node node-1 dedicated-   │
  │ 2. Add toleration to pod spec                           │
  │ 3. Reduce CPU requests or add more nodes               │
  │ 4. Check actual node capacity: kubectl describe node   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

2.4 Container Output Streams & LoggingQ57-Q68

Troubleshooting Q57 of 200
Why does the 12-Factor App methodology say "log to stdout, not files"?
A) stdout is faster than writing to files
B) Containers capture stdout/stderr automatically. If you write to files inside the container, those files are on the ephemeral writable layer (lost on restart) and inaccessible to kubectl logs. The platform (Kubernetes) should handle log routing, not the application
C) Writing to files requires root permissions which containers don't have
D) stdout logs are encrypted; file logs are not
✅ Correct Answer: B

When your Django app writes to stdout (print/logging.StreamHandler), Kubernetes captures it via the container runtime and makes it available through kubectl logs. If Django writes to /var/log/app.log, that file disappears when the pod restarts and you can't see it with kubectl logs.

📝 12-Factor Logging
12-Factor Logging
stdout vs File Logging
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ WRONG: Django → /var/log/app.log (inside container)     │
  │   ❌ Lost on restart  ❌ kubectl logs can't see it       │
  │                                                          │
  │ RIGHT: Django → stdout (console)                        │
  │   ✅ Captured by container runtime                       │
  │   ✅ kubectl logs shows it                               │
  │   ✅ Forwarded by Fluentd/Filebeat                       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  # Django logging config for Kubernetes:
  LOGGING = {
      'handlers': {
          'console': {
              'class': 'logging.StreamHandler',
              'stream': sys.stdout,  # ← THIS is the key
          },
      },
  }
Troubleshooting Q58 of 200
What does kubectl logs --follow do?
A) It downloads all historical logs to a file
B) It shows logs from all pods in the namespace
C) It streams logs in real-time (like tail -f). New log lines appear as they're written. Press Ctrl+C to stop
D) It follows the pod as it moves between nodes
✅ Correct Answer: C

Useful combinations: kubectl logs -f deploy/anihpj-api (stream all replicas), kubectl logs -f --tail=20 pod/anihpj-web-xxx (show last 20 lines then follow), kubectl logs -f --timestamps pod/anihpj-db-0 (show timestamps).

📝 kubectl logs --follow
kubectl logs --follow
Real-time Log Streaming
  kubectl logs -f deploy/anihpj-api    # Stream all replicas
  kubectl logs -f --tail=20 pod/x      # Last 20 + follow
  kubectl logs -f --timestamps pod/x   # With timestamps
  
  # Multi-container:
  kubectl logs -f pod/x -c nginx       # Specific container
  kubectl logs -f --all-containers pod/x # All containers
Troubleshooting Q59 of 200
What is the sidecar logging pattern?
A) A dedicated logging container runs alongside the app container in the SAME pod. The app writes logs to a shared volume (emptyDir), and the sidecar reads them and forwards to a logging backend (Fluentd, Filebeat). This decouples logging from the application
B) Running a separate pod for logging on each node
C) Using kubectl logs on a secondary terminal
D) The app container logs directly to an external service via HTTP
✅ Correct Answer: A

Sidecar pattern for anihpj: Django writes to stdout (captured by Kubernetes) AND to a file in emptyDir. A Fluentd sidecar reads the file and sends to Elasticsearch. The sidecar handles log rotation, batching, retries — Django doesn't need to know about Elasticsearch at all.

📝 Sidecar Logging Pattern
Sidecar Logging Pattern
anihpj with Fluentd Sidecar
  Pod: anihpj-api
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Container: api (Django)         │
  │   Writes to stdout              │
  │   + writes to /var/log/app/     │
  │     (emptyDir shared volume)    │
  │           │                     │
  │           ▼                     │
  │ Container: fluentd-sidecar      │
  │   Reads /var/log/app/*.log      │
  │   Forwards to Elasticsearch     │
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
  
  Benefit: Django doesn't need ES client library.
  Fluentd handles retries, batching, TLS.
Troubleshooting Q60 of 200
What controls log rotation for containers in Kubernetes?
A) Kubernetes has no log rotation — logs grow indefinitely
B) Each container must implement its own log rotation internally
C) The cloud provider handles log rotation automatically
D) The kubelet, via container runtime settings: containerLogMaxSize (max size per log file, e.g., "10Mi") and containerLogMaxFiles (number of rotated files to keep, e.g., 5). Configured in kubelet config or kubeadm ConfigMap
✅ Correct Answer: D

Default: containerLogMaxSize=10Mi, containerLogMaxFiles=5 (50Mi max per container). If your anihpj-api generates 100MB of logs per day, increase these values or set up centralized logging (EFK/Loki stack) to avoid log loss.

📝 Log Rotation Config
Log Rotation Config
Kubelet Log Rotation Settings
  # In /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml:
  containerLogMaxSize: "10Mi"    # Rotate when file > 10MiB
  containerLogMaxFiles: 5        # Keep 5 rotated files
  
  # Per container max: 10Mi * 5 = 50Mi
  
  # For anihpj with verbose Django logging:
  containerLogMaxSize: "50Mi"
  containerLogMaxFiles: 3
  # → 150Mi max per container
Troubleshooting Q61 of 200
What does kubectl get events show?
A) Only pod creation and deletion events
B) A cluster-wide chronological log of all significant actions: pod scheduling, image pulling, container starts/stops, node status changes, PVC binding, etc. Events are retained for 1 hour by default. Use --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' to see the most recent first
C) The same information as kubectl logs but formatted differently
D) Only error events — successful operations are not shown
✅ Correct Answer: B

Events are your cluster's audit trail. Use kubectl get events -n anihpj --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' to see what's happening in your namespace. Events older than 1 hour are automatically deleted by the kube-controller-manager.

Troubleshooting Q62 of 200
What are Kubernetes audit logs?
A) The same as kubectl logs — just a different name
B) Logs automatically generated for every pod restart
C) A detailed record of WHO did WHAT and WHEN — every API request (kubectl commands, controller actions) is logged. Useful for security forensics: "Who deleted the anihpj namespace?" Audit policy controls what's logged (RequestResponse, Request, None)
D) Logs sent to external cloud monitoring services only
✅ Correct Answer: C

Audit logs answer: Who ran kubectl delete secret anihpj-db-creds? Who modified the Deployment? Audit policy stages: RequestReceived, ResponseStarted, ResponseComplete, Panic. Configured via --audit-policy-file on kube-apiserver.

📝 Audit Logs
Audit Logs
Kubernetes Audit Log Levels
  LEVEL         LOGS WHAT
  ─────         ─────────
  None          Nothing
  Metadata      Request metadata (who, what, when)
                NOT request body
  Request       Metadata + request body
  RequestResponse Metadata + request body + response body
  
  # Audit policy example:
  apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
  kind: Policy
  rules:
  - level: RequestResponse
    verbs: ["delete"]
    resources: [{"group": "", "resource": "secrets"}]
  # → Logs every secret deletion with full request/response!

A) kubectl exec -it <pod> -- /bin/bash (or /bin/sh for Alpine-based images). The -it flags make it interactive with a TTY. This is your primary tool for in-container debugging
B) SSH to the node and docker exec into the container

D) You can only get a shell during pod creation — not on running pods
✅ Correct Answer: A

Essential debugging: kubectl exec -it anihpj-api-xxx -- /bin/bash. Then: check env vars (env | grep DATABASE), test connectivity (curl localhost:8000/health), check DNS (nslookup anihpj-db). For containers without bash: use /bin/sh or kubectl debug for ephemeral containers.

📝 kubectl exec
kubectl exec
Container Shell Access

  nslookup anihpj-db           # Test DNS
  cat /etc/resolv.conf         # Check DNS config

Troubleshooting Q66 of 200
What is kubectl debug (ephemeral containers)?
A) A command that fixes broken pods automatically
B) A verbose logging mode for kubectl
C) It injects a temporary (ephemeral) debugging container into a running pod. Useful when the pod's container is minimal (distroless, scratch) and has no shell. kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox --target=<container>
D) It creates a copy of the pod with root access for debugging
✅ Correct Answer: C

Ephemeral containers are added to running pods without restarting them. They share the pod's network and PID namespace, so you can run network tools (curl, nslookup, tcpdump) that aren't in the main container. Requires EphemeralContainers feature gate (enabled by default in 1.25+).

kubectl debug
Ephemeral Debug Containers

    --image=nicolaka/netshoot \
    --target=api

  # - curl, nslookup, tcpdump, netstat, ss
  # - Can see the target container's processes via /proc
  
  # The debug container is temporary:
  # - Removed when you exit
  # - Doesn't restart the pod
  # - Doesn't appear in pod spec

B) A Kubernetes-native logging system built into the kubelet

Troubleshooting Q68 of 200
You run kubectl logs anihpj-api-xxx and get no output, but the pod is Running and serving traffic. Why?
A) kubectl logs is broken — use journalctl instead
B) The pod is using a non-standard logging driver
C) Logs are only available for the first 10 minutes of a pod's life
D) The application is writing logs to a FILE instead of stdout/stderr. kubectl logs only captures stdout/stderr streams. Fix: configure Django to use logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout) instead of FileHandler
✅ Correct Answer: D

This is a common Django mistake. Django's default logging writes to console (which the dev server shows), but in production with Gunicorn, you need explicit StreamHandler configuration. Verify: kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -- ls /var/log/app.log — if the file exists, the app is logging to files, not stdout.

Why kubectl logs Returns Nothing

  4. Check previous container (if restarted):

     LOGGING['handlers']['console']['stream'] = sys.stdout

2.5 Services & Networking TroubleshootingQ69-Q80

Troubleshooting Q69 of 200
A pod cannot resolve anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. What is the FIRST thing to check?
A) Restart all CoreDNS pods
B) Check /etc/resolv.conf inside the pod (kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf). The nameserver should point to CoreDNS (usually 10.96.0.10). If it points elsewhere or has wrong search domains, DNS resolution fails
C) Immediately reboot the worker node
D) Delete and recreate the pod — DNS will fix itself
✅ Correct Answer: B

The pod's /etc/resolv.conf is configured by kubelet based on the pod's dnsPolicy. Check: nameserver line (should be CoreDNS ClusterIP), search line (should include namespace and cluster domain). For anihpj: search anihpj.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local.

📝 DNS Debugging
DNS Debugging
Pod DNS Checklist
  kubectl exec anihpj-api-xxx -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
  
  nameserver 10.96.0.10          ← CoreDNS ClusterIP
  search anihpj.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
  options ndots:5
  
  # Test DNS resolution:
  kubectl exec pod -- nslookup anihpj-db
  kubectl exec pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default
  
  # Test CoreDNS directly:
  kubectl exec pod -- nslookup anihpj-db 10.96.0.10
Troubleshooting Q70 of 200
What is CoreDNS in Kubernetes, and where is its configuration stored?
A) CoreDNS is an external DNS service — configuration is in AWS Route53
B) CoreDNS is a pod that caches external DNS only — no configuration needed
C) CoreDNS is the cluster DNS server (replaced kube-dns). It resolves Service names to ClusterIPs. Configuration is in the coredns ConfigMap in kube-system namespace, using the Corefile format
D) CoreDNS configuration is embedded in the container image and can't be changed
✅ Correct Answer: C

CoreDNS ConfigMap (kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml) contains the Corefile. Key plugins: kubernetes (cluster domain resolution), forward (upstream DNS for external names), cache (performance), errors (logging), health (probe endpoint).

📝 CoreDNS ConfigMap
CoreDNS ConfigMap
CoreDNS Corefile (kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml)
  .:53 {
      errors         # Log errors
      health         # Health check endpoint :8080/health
      ready          # Readiness endpoint :8181/ready
      kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
          pods insecure
          fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
      }
      prometheus :9153
      forward . /etc/resolv.conf  # Upstream DNS
      cache 30                    # Cache for 30s
      loop
      reload
      loadbalance
  }
Troubleshooting Q71 of 200
What is ndots in /etc/resolv.conf and why does it matter for Kubernetes?
A) ndots controls when the DNS search domain is appended. Default ndots:5 means any name with fewer than 5 dots gets search domains appended first. This can cause excessive DNS queries in Kubernetes where service names have 3+ dots (anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local has 4 dots!)
B) ndots controls how many DNS servers are queried in parallel
C) ndots is a network bandwidth setting — unrelated to DNS
D) ndots controls DNS caching TTL values
✅ Correct Answer: A

With ndots:5, resolving anihpj-api causes 5 DNS lookups (one for each search domain) before trying the name as-is. With ndots:1, it's only 1 lookup. For Kubernetes, consider setting ndots:2 or using FQDN (anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.) to avoid the search list entirely.

📝 ndots & DNS Performance
ndots & DNS Performance
ndots:5 Problem
  Resolving "anihpj-api" with ndots:5:
  Query 1: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
  Query 2: anihpj-api.svc.cluster.local
  Query 3: anihpj-api.cluster.local
  Query 4: anihpj-api  (finally tries without search!)
  
  = 4 DNS queries for ONE name!
  
  FIX: Use FQDN: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. (trailing dot)
  OR: Set ndots:2 in pod dnsConfig for better performance
Troubleshooting Q72 of 200
What does dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet do?
A) It disables DNS for hostNetwork pods
B) It forwards all DNS queries to the host's DNS server
C) It makes the pod use the node's DNS configuration
D) For pods using hostNetwork, by default they use the NODE's DNS (dnsPolicy=Default). ClusterFirstWithHostNet forces them to use CoreDNS instead — useful for DaemonSet pods that need cluster DNS resolution while using hostNetwork
✅ Correct Answer: D

dnsPolicy options: ClusterFirst (default — use CoreDNS), Default (use node's /etc/resolv.conf), None (custom DNS config via dnsConfig), ClusterFirstWithHostNet (CoreDNS for hostNetwork pods). CNI plugins often use hostNetwork and need ClusterFirstWithHostNet.

📝 dnsPolicy Options
dnsPolicy Options
dnsPolicy Values
  POLICY                    BEHAVIOR
  ──────                    ───────
  ClusterFirst (default)    Use CoreDNS for all queries
  Default                   Use node's /etc/resolv.conf
  ClusterFirstWithHostNet   Use CoreDNS even with hostNetwork
  None                      Custom DNS via dnsConfig field
  
  # Custom DNS example:
  dnsPolicy: None
  dnsConfig:
    nameservers:
    - 8.8.8.8
    searches:
    - mydomain.local
Troubleshooting Q73 of 200
You create a Service but kubectl get endpoints shows no endpoints. What's wrong?
A) The Service type must be LoadBalancer for endpoints to appear
B) The Service's selector doesn't match any pod's labels. Check: kubectl get pods --selector=<service-selector>. If 0 pods match, the endpoints list is empty and the Service routes nowhere
C) Endpoints are deprecated — use EndpointSlices instead
D) You need to wait 30 minutes for endpoints to populate
✅ Correct Answer: B

Selector mismatch is the #1 cause of "Service doesn't work." Verify: kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj,tier=api. If the pod has tier: ap1 but the Service selector says tier: api — no match, no endpoints. Use kubectl describe svc to see the selector and compare with pod labels.

📝 Service No Endpoints
Service No Endpoints
Debug Selector Mismatch
  # 1. Check Service selector:
  kubectl describe svc anihpj-api | grep Selector
  Selector: app=anihpj,tier=api
  
  # 2. Check if pods match:
  kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj,tier=api
  NAME              READY   STATUS
  anihpj-api-xxx    1/1     Running
  
  # 3. Common mismatch:
  Service selector: tier=api
  Pod labels:       tier=ap1  ← TYPO! No match!
  
  # 4. Check endpoints:
  kubectl get endpoints anihpj-api
  # Empty list = selector mismatch!
Troubleshooting Q74 of 200
What is the difference between kube-proxy iptables mode and IPVS mode?
A) There is no difference — they are aliases for the same code
B) iptables mode works only on Linux; IPVS works only on Windows
C) iptables: sequential rule matching (O(n) — slow with many services). IPVS: kernel-level hash table load balancing (O(1) — fast regardless of service count). IPVS also supports more load balancing algorithms (rr, lc, dh, sh, sed, nq)
D) iptables is the newer, recommended mode; IPVS is legacy
✅ Correct Answer: C

For clusters with 1000+ services, iptables mode becomes slow (every packet traverses thousands of rules). IPVS uses a hash table for instant backend lookup. Cilium takes this further by replacing kube-proxy entirely with eBPF-based load balancing — even faster than IPVS.

📝 kube-proxy iptables vs IPVS
kube-proxy iptables vs IPVS
kube-proxy Modes Comparison
  MODE        MECHANISM         PERFORMANCE    LOAD BALANCE
  ────        ─────────         ───────────    ───────────
  iptables    Sequential rules   O(n) slow     Random only
              (thousands of      with many
               rules)            services
  ────        ─────────         ───────────    ───────────
  IPVS        Kernel hash table  O(1) fast     rr, lc, dh,
                                          sh, sed, nq
  Check mode: kubectl logs -n kube-system ds/kube-proxy | grep "Using"
Troubleshooting Q75 of 200
How do you debug NetworkPolicy issues in a pod?
A) Use kubectl describe networkpolicy to see the policy rules, then test connectivity from within the pod using tools like nc -zv <target> <port> or curl. Check the CNI plugin logs for policy enforcement logs
B) NetworkPolicies can't be debugged — they either work or don't
C) Use kubectl debug-networkpolicy — a built-in debugging tool
D) Delete all policies and reapply one by one until you find the problem
✅ Correct Answer: A

Systematic approach: (1) kubectl describe netpol to see rules. (2) Check pod labels match selectors. (3) Test from source pod: nc -vz target-ip port. (4) If using Calico: calicoctl ipam check. (5) If using Cilium: hubble observe --verdict DROPPED.

📝 NetworkPolicy Debugging
NetworkPolicy Debugging
Systematic Policy Testing
  # 1. List all policies:
  kubectl get netpol -A
  
  # 2. Check policy details:
  kubectl describe netpol deny-all -n anihpj
  
  # 3. Test from a debug pod:
  kubectl run test --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash
  curl anihpj-api.anihpj.svc:8000/health
  nc -vz anihpj-db.anihpj.svc 5432
  
  # 4. With Cilium:
  hubble observe --from-pod ns/web --to-pod ns/api --verdict DROPPED
Troubleshooting Q76 of 200
What is the CNI configuration directory and why does it matter for troubleshooting?
A) /etc/kubernetes/cni — stores CNI binaries
B) CNI is configured through the Kubernetes API only — no filesystem config
C) /opt/cni/bin — stores CNI plugin executables only
D) /etc/cni/net.d/ — contains JSON config files specifying which CNI plugin to use and its settings. If multiple configs exist, the first alphabetically wins. A misconfigured or old config here can break pod networking entirely
✅ Correct Answer: D

Common issue: migrating from one CNI to another leaves old configs in /etc/cni/net.d/. Example: 10-calico.conflist and 10-flannel.conflist both exist — kubelet picks the first one, but the plugin binary for the other is still installed. Result: broken networking.

📝 CNI Config Directory
CNI Config Directory
/etc/cni/net.d/ Structure
  ls /etc/cni/net.d/
  10-calico.conflist       ← Calico config (JSON)
  05-cilium.conflist       ← Cilium config (takes priority!)
  
  Kubelet picks FIRST alphabetically!
  Migration issue: old CNI config left behind
  → kubelet loads wrong plugin
  → pods can't get IPs
  
  FIX: Remove old CNI configs before installing new CNI

Troubleshooting Q78 of 200
What is the pod network connectivity checklist for systematic debugging?
A) There is no checklist — every issue is unique
B) Just run kubectl describe pod and you'll find the problem
C) 1. Pod exists and is Running? 2. Pod has an IP? (kubectl get pod -o wide) 3. Can pod reach itself? (curl localhost:port) 4. Can pod reach another pod by IP? 5. Can pod resolve DNS? (nslookup service-name) 6. Can pod reach a Service? (curl service-name:port) 7. NetworkPolicies? (kubectl get netpol)
D) Check the node's /var/log/messages file
✅ Correct Answer: C

Work through the OSI layers: Layer 3 (IP) → Layer 4 (TCP) → Layer 7 (DNS/HTTP). Each step isolates the problem. If IP-to-IP works but DNS doesn't → CoreDNS issue. If nothing works → CNI issue. If Service doesn't work but pod IP does → kube-proxy or selector issue.

📝 Network Connectivity Checklist
Network Connectivity Checklist
7-Layer Debugging Approach
  LAYER  TEST                              COMMAND
  ─────  ────                              ───────
  1. Pod  Is pod Running? Has IP?          kubectl get pod -o wide
  2. Self Can pod reach itself?            curl localhost:8000
  3. IP   Can pod ping another pod IP?     ping 10.0.2.9
  4. DNS  Can pod resolve Service name?    nslookup anihpj-api
  5. Svc  Can pod reach Service?           curl svc-name:port
  6. Ext  Can pod reach internet?          curl google.com
  7. Pol  Any NetworkPolicies blocking?    kubectl get netpol
  
  WORK THROUGH LAYERS BOTTOM-UP!
Troubleshooting Q79 of 200
How does kube-proxy (iptables mode) handle Service traffic?
A) kube-proxy watches the API server for Service and Endpoint changes, then programs iptables rules on each node. When a pod sends traffic to a Service ClusterIP, iptables DNAT rules rewrite the destination to a random backend pod IP (statistically distributed)
B) kube-proxy runs as a proxy server that all traffic passes through
C) kube-proxy uses DNS round-robin to distribute traffic
D) kube-proxy only works with LoadBalancer services
✅ Correct Answer: A

kube-proxy is NOT a proxy — it's a rule programmer. It writes iptables rules that the kernel executes directly. This means there's no extra network hop: traffic goes pod → kernel iptables → destination pod. The rules are in the NAT table: iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES.

📝 kube-proxy iptables Rules
kube-proxy iptables Rules
How iptables DNAT Routes Service Traffic
  # View Service rules:
  iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES -n
  
  Chain KUBE-SERVICES
  target     prot  opt  source    destination
  KUBE-SVC-  tcp   --   0.0.0.0/0 10.96.100.50  tcp dpt:8000
  
  # Traffic flow:
  Pod → Service ClusterIP (10.96.100.50:8000)
    → iptables DNAT rewrites to random pod IP
    → Pod receives traffic directly (no proxy hop!)
Troubleshooting Q80 of 200
A pod can reach the internet but cannot reach another pod in a DIFFERENT namespace. What should you check?
A) The pod needs a ClusterRole to access cross-namespace pods
B) Cross-namespace pod communication is disabled by default in Kubernetes
C) You need to create a Service in the target namespace first
D) Check for NetworkPolicies in the TARGET namespace that might block ingress from the source namespace. Also check the pod is using the correct DNS name: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Without the namespace qualifier, DNS resolves to the source pod's own namespace
✅ Correct Answer: D

Two key checks: (1) NetworkPolicy — a default-deny policy in the target namespace blocks all ingress unless explicitly allowed. (2) DNS — anihpj-api resolves to anihpj-api.<current-ns>.svc. Use the FQDN: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local for cross-namespace access.

📝 Cross-Namespace Communication
Cross-Namespace Communication
Cross-Namespace DNS
  # From default namespace → anihpj namespace:
  
  WRONG: anihpj-api (resolves in CURRENT namespace)
  RIGHT: anihpj-api.anihpj.svc.cluster.local (FQDN)
  
  # Check for NetworkPolicies in target namespace:
  kubectl get netpol -n anihpj
  
  # Allow ingress from another namespace:
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: monitoring

⚙️ Category 3: Workloads & Scheduling (15%)Q81-Q110

🟡 Running Applications — Deployments, ConfigMaps, Autoscaling, Scheduling

This category is about running your applications: deploying them, updating without downtime, configuring them, and ensuring they land on the right nodes. For anihpj/jobpost, this means rolling out new API versions without dropping traffic, managing DB passwords via Secrets, auto-scaling during traffic spikes, and ensuring pods are spread across availability zones.

Q81-Q11030 Questions🟡 Intermediate

3.1 Deployments, Rolling Updates & RollbacksQ81-Q90

Workloads Q81 of 200
What is the Kubernetes object hierarchy for running an application: Deployment → ? → Pod?
A) Deployment → Service → Pod
B) Deployment → StatefulSet → Pod
C) Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod. The Deployment manages ReplicaSets (one per revision), and each ReplicaSet ensures N identical pods are running
D) Deployment directly manages Pods — there is no intermediate object
✅ Correct Answer: C

Deployment creates ReplicaSets. ReplicaSets create Pods. When you update a Deployment, it creates a NEW ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling down the old one. This is why kubectl get rs shows multiple ReplicaSets after updates — each represents a revision.

Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod Hierarchy
  Deployment: anihpj-api (desired: 3 replicas, image: anihpj/jobpost:v2)
  │
  ├─ ReplicaSet: anihpj-api-v1 (revision 1)
  │   ├─ Pod: anihpj-api-v1-abc (running v1)
  │   └─ Pod: anihpj-api-v1-def (running v1)  ← scaling DOWN during rollout
  │
  └─ ReplicaSet: anihpj-api-v2 (revision 2)
      ├─ Pod: anihpj-api-v2-ghi (running v2)  ← scaling UP during rollout
      ├─ Pod: anihpj-api-v2-jkl (running v2)
      └─ Pod: anihpj-api-v2-mno (running v2)
Workloads Q82 of 200
What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control in a rolling update?
A) maxSurge = how many EXTRA pods can be created ABOVE the desired count during rollout (e.g., 25% = up to 125% total). maxUnavailable = how many pods can be UNAVAILABLE during rollout (e.g., 25% = at least 75% available). Together they control the speed vs safety tradeoff
B) maxSurge = max CPU usage; maxUnavailable = max memory usage
C) maxSurge = max pods per node; maxUnavailable = min pods per node
D) They are Kubernetes autoscaling parameters, not for deployments
✅ Correct Answer: A

With 10 replicas, maxSurge=25% (2.5→3), maxUnavailable=25% (2.5→2): During rollout, Kubernetes can create up to 13 pods total (10 desired + 3 surge) and allows up to 2 pods to be unavailable. This means at least 8 pods always serve traffic. For anihpj-api (3 replicas): set maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0 for zero-downtime.

📝 maxSurge/maxUnavailable
maxSurge/maxUnavailable
Rolling Update Math
  10 replicas, maxSurge=25%, maxUnavailable=25%

  maxSurge: ceil(10 * 0.25) = 3 extra pods allowed
  maxUnavailable: floor(10 * 0.25) = 2 pods can be down
  
  During rollout: up to 13 pods total, at least 8 available
  
  For anihpj-api (3 replicas, zero-downtime):
  maxSurge: 1
  maxUnavailable: 0  ← Never drop below 3 pods!
Workloads Q83 of 200
How do you rollback a Deployment to a previous version?
A) Delete and recreate the Deployment with the old image
B) kubectl apply -f old-deployment.yaml
C) You can't — once updated, Deployments can't be rolled back
D) kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj-api — rolls back to the PREVIOUS revision. Use --to-revision=N to roll back to a specific revision. Check available revisions with kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj-api
✅ Correct Answer: D

Rollout undo is instant because the old ReplicaSet still exists (just scaled to 0). Kubernetes simply scales up the old ReplicaSet and scales down the current one. The revisionHistoryLimit (default 10) controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept for rollbacks.

  kubectl rollout undo deploy/anihpj-api --to-revision=2  # Specific rev
  
  kubectl rollout status deploy/anihpj-api  # Watch progress

What is the difference between Blue-Green and Canary deployment strategies?
A) They are the same — different names for the same pattern
B) Blue-Green uses canary pods; Canary uses blue-green pods
C) Blue-Green: TWO complete environments (old "blue", new "green"). Switch ALL traffic at once by updating the Service selector. Canary: gradually shift a PERCENTAGE of traffic to the new version (10% → 25% → 50% → 100%), monitoring for errors at each step
D) Blue-Green is for databases; Canary is for web applications
✅ Correct Answer: C

Blue-Green: Simple, fast rollback (switch Service back to blue). Requires 2x resources. Canary: Gradual, safer (catch errors with small % of traffic). Requires traffic splitting (Ingress/Gateway API/Service Mesh). For anihpj: Blue-Green for database schema changes, Canary for API code changes.

What does kubectl rollout pause and kubectl rollout resume do?

B) Pause: Stops all pods. Resume: Restarts them
C) Pause: Takes a snapshot. Resume: Restores from snapshot
D) These commands don't exist — they are from Docker, not Kubernetes
✅ Correct Answer: A

Scenario: You update the image to v2-canary and pause. The canary pod runs. You monitor for 5 minutes. All good → resume. Issues found → undo without the canary having progressed to full rollout. This gives you a manual canary without needing traffic splitting infrastructure.

📝 Rollout Pause/Resume
Rollout Pause/Resume
Manual Canary with Pause
  kubectl set image deploy/anihpj-api *=v2-canary
  kubectl rollout pause deploy/anihpj-api
  
  # Canary pod is now running alongside v1 pods
  # Monitor for 5 min:
  kubectl logs -f deploy/anihpj-api | grep ERROR
  
  # All good → resume:
  kubectl rollout resume deploy/anihpj-api

B) kubectl logs deployment/anihpj-api
C) kubectl rollout restart deployment/anihpj-api
D) kubectl describe deployment — shows Conditions (Available, Progressing) and the rollout status. Then kubectl describe rs to see the new ReplicaSet, and kubectl describe pod on new pods to find the root cause (ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, insufficient resources)

Systematic rollout debugging: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod. Start at the top: kubectl describe deploy tells you if the rollout is progressing. If new ReplicaSet isn't scaling up, check its pods. If pods are pending, check scheduler events. If pods crash, check logs.

  kubectl describe deploy → "Progressing: False"

Workloads Q88 of 200
What does revisionHistoryLimit in a Deployment spec control?
A) How many pods can be created per minute
B) How many OLD ReplicaSets to keep for rollback purposes (default: 10). Setting it to 0 means you cannot rollback. Setting it too high wastes etcd storage and clutters kubectl get rs output
C) How many times a pod can restart before being evicted
D) The maximum number of concurrent rollouts in the cluster
✅ Correct Answer: B

Each ReplicaSet stores the full pod template. With revisionHistoryLimit=10 and frequent deployments, you could have 10+ old ReplicaSets. For CI/CD environments deploying every 5 minutes, set this to 3-5 to keep the cluster clean. Zero means no rollback possible.

📝 revisionHistoryLimit
revisionHistoryLimit
revisionHistoryLimit: 10  ← default
  Each RS stores full pod template in etcd.
  
  With CI/CD deploying every 5 min:
  10 RS × 5 min = 50 min of rollback history
  After 11th deploy, oldest RS is deleted.
  
  Set to 3-5 for CI/CD, 10 for manual deployments.

How does a Service know which pods to route traffic to during a rolling update?
A) The Service is updated by the Deployment controller during rollout
B) Services use pod names, not labels, to find backends
C) Services use LABEL SELECTORS — they match ALL pods (old and new) that have matching labels. During a rolling update, both old and new pods have the same labels, so the Service routes to both. Readiness probes ensure only healthy pods receive traffic
D) The Service temporarily stops routing during a rollout
✅ Correct Answer: C

This is why rolling updates work with zero downtime: the Service sees all pods with matching labels. Old pods continue serving until new pods pass readiness probes and are added to the Service endpoints. For anihpj-api: ensure readiness probe checks the /health endpoint so new pods are only added when truly ready.

  NEW pods: app=anihpj,tier=api ✅ Matches → receives traffic
  
  Both old and new pods have SAME labels!

C) ConfigMap is a cloud storage service like S3

✅ Correct Answer: B

If you update a ConfigMap, do pods automatically pick up the changes?
A) No — pods do NOT auto-restart. Changes to ConfigMaps mounted as ENV vars are only picked up on pod restart. Changes to ConfigMaps mounted as VOLUMES may be reflected after a delay (kubelet sync period, ~60-90s), but the APPLICATION must re-read the file
B) Yes — pods automatically restart when ConfigMaps change
C) Yes — but only for Deployments, not StatefulSets
D) ConfigMaps are immutable and can never be updated after creation
✅ Correct Answer: A

This is a common gotcha. You update a ConfigMap, but pods keep using the old values. Solutions: (1) Use kubectl rollout restart deploy/anihpj-api to trigger a rolling restart. (2) Use stakater/Reloader which watches ConfigMaps and auto-restarts pods. (3) Mount as volume + implement file watchers in your app.

Why Pods Don't Auto-Restart

Secret Base64 Encoding

What does immutable: true on a ConfigMap or Secret do?

B) Makes the data encrypted and unreadable by users

What is HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) and how does it work?
A) HPA adds more NODES to the cluster when CPU is high
B) HPA automatically adjusts the number of POD replicas based on CPU/memory/custom metrics. Formula: desiredReplicas = ceil[currentReplicas * (currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue)]. It queries metrics-server every 15s
C) HPA adjusts the CPU and memory limits of existing pods
D) HPA stands for "High Performance Architecture" and optimizes pod placement
✅ Correct Answer: B

HPA for anihpj-api: kubectl autoscale deploy anihpj-api --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70. When average CPU across pods exceeds 70%, HPA adds pods. Requires metrics-server and resource requests set on containers.

📝 HPA Command
HPA Command
kubectl autoscale
  kubectl autoscale deploy anihpj-api \
    --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
  
  kubectl get hpa anihpj-api
  NAME          REFERENCE          TARGETS   MIN  MAX  REPLICAS
  anihpj-api    Deployment/api     45%/70%   2    10   3
  
  # HPA uses ceil[current * (currentMetric/desiredMetric)]
  # If average CPU=90% and target=70%:
  # desiredReplicas = ceil[3 * (90/70)] = ceil[3.86] = 4
