  3. RBAC aggregated ClusterRoles not updated: Custom roles extending built-in roles not refreshed.
  4. RBAC API version mismatch: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 vs v1beta1.
  5. Impersonation headers stripped by proxy: --as flag doesn't work behind corporate proxy.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. No RBAC configured: Cluster runs with --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow (insecure).
  2. system:masters group overused: Everyone added to admin group instead of granular RBAC.
  3. No ClusterRole aggregator labels: Custom ClusterRoles not picking up new APIs automatically.
  4. Default RBAC from kubeadm: Only cluster-admin exists, no namespace-level roles.
  5. New namespace: No default RBAC setup — users have zero access to new namespaces.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl auth can-i --list --as=<user> -n <ns>. kubectl get rolebinding,clusterrolebinding -A -o wide.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n <ns>
2. kubectl create rolebinding alice-pod --role=pod-reader --user=alice -n <ns>
3. Verify: kubectl auth can-i get pods --as=alice -n <ns>
4. For cluster-wide: use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
5. For SAs: kubectl create rolebinding sa-pod --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=<ns>:<sa>

💡 Personal Advice: RBAC troubleshooting = kubectl auth can-i is your best friend. It impersonates any user/SA and tests permissions. On CKA: you'll create Roles, RoleBindings, ClusterRoles, and ClusterRoleBindings. Know the difference: Role=namespaced, ClusterRole=cluster-wide. RoleBinding can bind EITHER; ClusterRoleBinding binds ONLY ClusterRoles.

📌 CA16–CA25: Extensibility — Helm, CRDs, Operators, Webhooks

CA16
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA16
Helm Release Failed — Install/Upgrade Error

🔍 Symptom: helm install or helm upgrade fails with "rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists" or template error.

$ helm install my-app ./chart
❌ Error: rendered manifests contain a resource that already exists
❌ Error: cannot re-use a name that is still in use
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Resource already exists from previous failed install: helm list -A — release may be in failed state.
  2. Template rendering error: Invalid Go template syntax in chart templates. helm template ./chart --debug.
  3. values.yaml has wrong structure: Missing required values or wrong YAML indentation.
  4. Previous release not fully deleted: Secrets (Helm 3) or ConfigMaps (Helm 2) still present.
  5. Namespace doesn't exist: helm install --create-namespace or pre-create namespace.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Helm version incompatibility: Chart requires Helm 3.7+ but cluster has 3.2.
  2. CRDs not installed before chart: Chart requires CRDs that must be applied first.
  3. Helm hook failed: pre-install/pre-upgrade hook pod crashed, blocking release.
  4. RBAC: ServiceAccount used by Helm doesn't have permission to create resources.
  5. Helm repository index stale: helm repo update not run.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First Helm install: helm repo add and helm repo update must be done first.
  2. Helm 3 stores releases as Secrets: Need permission to create/get Secrets in the namespace.
  3. --atomic flag not used: Failed install leaves partial resources. Use --atomic for auto-rollback.
  4. No default StorageClass: PVC in chart can't provision — blocks install.
  5. Helm diff not run: helm diff upgrade would catch issues before applying.
🔍 What to Look At: helm list -A and helm history <release>. helm template ./chart --debug. kubectl get events -n <ns>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. helm uninstall <release> -n <ns> to clean failed release
2. helm template ./chart --debug to validate templates
3. helm install --create-namespace --atomic <name> ./chart
4. Check RBAC: ServiceAccount needs appropriate permissions
5. helm rollback <release> <rev> if upgrade failed

💡 Personal Advice: Helm failures are usually: (1) existing resource conflict — uninstall first, (2) template error — use helm template --debug, or (3) RBAC — your kubeconfig user needs cluster-admin or specific permissions. On CKA: Helm is tested — know install, upgrade, rollback, and troubleshooting with helm list/history/status.
CA17
🔧 CATEGORY CA — Issue CA17
CRD Not Working — Custom Resource Not Recognized

🔍 Symptom: kubectl apply -f my-cr.yaml fails with "no matches for kind." CRD is not installed or the API group/version is wrong.

$ kubectl apply -f my-cr.yaml
❌ error: unable to recognize "my-cr.yaml": no matches for kind "MySQL" in version "db.example.com/v1"

$ kubectl get crd
No resources found  ← CRD not installed!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. CRD not installed: kubectl get crd — must see the CRD definition. Apply CRD YAML first.
  2. API group/version mismatch: CR uses db.example.com/v1 but CRD defines v1alpha1.
  3. Kind name mismatch: CR uses kind: MySQLCluster but CRD defines kind: MySQL.
  4. CRD installed but not yet ready: New CRD takes a few seconds to register. Wait and retry.
  5. Schema validation fails: CR doesn't match CRD's openAPIV3Schema — required fields missing.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CRD in wrong scope: Namespaced CRD but CR doesn't specify namespace.
  2. CR references CRD from different API service: Aggregated API not registered.
  3. CRD conversion webhook failing: v1alpha1→v1 conversion not working — CR stuck.
  4. Multiple CRDs with overlapping group/version/kind — API server picks wrong one.
  5. CRD finalizer blocking CR creation: cleanup finalizer from previous CR stuck.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First CRD deployment: Apply CRD BEFORE any CRs. Order matters.
  2. CRD without controller: CR created but no operator watching — no pods/deployments created.
  3. CRD validation schema too strict: Prevents valid configurations.
  4. CRD versioning: v1beta1 CRD API deprecated in K8s 1.22 — must use apiextensions/v1.
  5. No CRD documentation: kubectl explain <resource> doesn't work without CRD.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get crd and kubectl describe crd <name>. kubectl api-resources | grep <kind>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get crd — verify CRD exists
2. kubectl describe crd <name> | grep -A5 Versions — check version names
3. Fix CR YAML: match kind, apiVersion exactly to CRD
4. kubectl apply -f crd.yaml then wait 5s, then apply CR
5. kubectl explain <resource> --recursive to see schema

💡 Personal Advice: CRDs extend Kubernetes — you're literally creating new API types. The CR must match the CRD exactly. On CKA: you may need to create a CRD and then a CR. Know: CRD defines the schema, CR is the instance, and a Controller (Operator) implements the logic. CRD alone does nothing — you need a controller for actual functionality.

🌐 Category 5: Services & Networking (20 Issues)SN1-SN20

🔴 Service Failures, DNS, Network Policies, Ingress

Networking is 20% of the CKA. Service-to-pod communication, CoreDNS, NetworkPolicies, and Ingress controllers are the most common failure points in production clusters.

📌 SN1–SN5: Service Communication Failures

SN1
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN1
Service Not Accessible — ClusterIP Returns Connection Refused

🔍 Symptom: Pod can't reach a Service by its DNS name. curl <svc>:<port> returns "connection refused" or times out. Service exists but isn't routing traffic.

$ kubectl exec web-pod -- curl api-svc:8080
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect: Connection refused

$ kubectl get endpoints api-svc
❌ api-svc       ← No endpoints!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Service has no Endpoints: kubectl get endpoints <svc> — empty means no pods match selector.
  2. Pod selector mismatch: Service selector != pod labels. One character off = no match.
  3. Pod not Ready: Pod is Running but Readiness probe failing — not added to Endpoints.
  4. Wrong namespace: Service in "default", pod calling from "dev" — different namespaces.
  5. Service port name doesn't match pod containerPort name: When using named ports.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. kube-proxy not running on node: iptables/IPVS rules not programmed — no DNAT happens.
  2. NetworkPolicy blocks ingress to backend pods from the source pod.
  3. Service type LoadBalancer with externalTrafficPolicy: Local — only routes to local pods.
  4. iptables rules corrupted: kube-proxy rules not updated after Service/pod changes.
  5. Service ClusterIP range conflict: Overlaps with pod CIDR — routing loops.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Service created before pods: No matching pods exist yet.
  2. kube-proxy mode mismatch: iptables vs IPVS — different behavior on different nodes.
  3. Service without selector: Manual Endpoints not created — Service has no targets.
  4. CoreDNS not resolving Service name: Service exists but DNS returns no IP.
  5. Headless Service (clusterIP: None) — DNS returns pod IPs directly, no ClusterIP.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get endpoints <svc>. kubectl get pods -l <selector> --show-labels. kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup <svc>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get endpoints <svc> — must show pod IPs
2. Compare: Service selector vs pod labels (--show-labels)
3. Check pod readiness: kubectl get pods — must show READY 1/1
4. Fix label mismatch: kubectl label pod <name> app=api --overwrite
5. Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -- curl <svc-ip>:<port>

💡 Personal Advice: Empty Endpoints = THE #1 Service issue. The Service selector and pod labels must match EXACTLY. Case matters. On CKA: you'll debug a Service that doesn't work. Run kubectl get endpoints first — empty = label mismatch or pod not Ready. Fix labels and endpoints populate in seconds.
SN2
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN2
NodePort Service Not Accessible Externally

🔍 Symptom: Service type NodePort created but curl <node-ip>:<nodeport> times out from outside the cluster. Port not reachable from external network.

$ kubectl get svc web-svc
NAME      TYPE       CLUSTER-IP    PORT(S)
web-svc   NodePort   10.96.0.50    80:30080/TCP

$ curl http://worker-ip:30080
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect: Connection refused
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Firewall blocking NodePort range (30000-32767): Cloud security group or host firewall.
  2. kube-proxy not running: iptables rule for NodePort not created. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-NODEPORTS.
  3. Node IP not reachable: Using internal IP instead of external/public IP.
  4. externalTrafficPolicy: Local — traffic dropped if no local pod on that node.
  5. Container not listening on 0.0.0.0: App bound to localhost only, can't receive external traffic.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI plugin doesn't support NodePort: Some overlay networks filter NodePort traffic.
  2. NodePort conflict with another service: Two Services using same NodePort.
  3. iptables rules not updated: kube-proxy hasn't synced after Service creation.
  4. Kubelet port range exhausted: All NodePorts in 30000-32767 already allocated.
  5. Cloud provider NAT translating NodePort traffic incorrectly.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First NodePort Service: Need to open firewall for 30000-32767 on ALL worker nodes.
  2. Node has no external IP: Private cluster — nodes only have internal IPs.
  3. kube-proxy mode: IPVS handles NodePort differently than iptables.
  4. Service created without proper selector: No backend pods = NodePort still opens but returns 503.
  5. Cloud LoadBalancer also created: External traffic going to LB, not directly to NodePort.
🔍 What to Look At: netstat -tlnp | grep <nodeport> on the node. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-NODEPORTS. curl localhost:<nodeport> on the node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Test locally on node: curl localhost:30080 — confirms Service works
2. Check firewall: iptables -L INPUT | grep 30080 — must allow
3. Cloud: open security group for port 30080 from 0.0.0.0/0
4. Use correct IP: Node's EXTERNAL/PUBLIC IP, not internal
5. kubectl get svc -o wide — verify NodePort assigned

💡 Personal Advice: NodePort works INSIDE the cluster but fails externally 90% of the time due to firewall/security groups. On CKA: you'll create a NodePort Service and need to access it. Test locally first (curl localhost:nodeport), then from external. If local works but external doesn't — it's ALWAYS the firewall.
SN3
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN3
LoadBalancer Service Stuck Pending — No External IP

🔍 Symptom: Service type LoadBalancer shows EXTERNAL-IP <pending> indefinitely. Cloud controller can't provision a load balancer. On bare metal without MetalLB.

$ kubectl get svc web-svc
NAME      TYPE           CLUSTER-IP    EXTERNAL-IP   PORT(S)
web-svc   LoadBalancer   10.96.0.50    <pending>     80:30080/TCP

$ kubectl describe svc web-svc
⚠️  Warning  CreatingLoadBalancerFailed  Error creating load balancer
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Bare metal/on-prem: No cloud-controller-manager — LoadBalancer requires MetalLB or similar.
  2. Cloud credentials missing: AWS/GCP/Azure credentials not configured for cloud-controller-manager.
  3. Insufficient cloud permissions: IAM role for CP nodes lacks ELB/NLB creation permissions.
  4. Cloud quota exceeded: Maximum number of LBs per region/account reached.
  5. Subnet configuration wrong: Cloud LB requires public subnets for internet-facing, private for internal.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Cloud controller pod not running: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cloud-controller.
  2. Service annotations misconfigured: Wrong annotation format for cloud-specific LB settings.
  3. Multiple LBs with same name: Naming conflict in cloud provider.
  4. Network tags on nodes missing: Cloud LB targets nodes by tag — tag not applied.
  5. Stale LoadBalancer: Previous LB not cleaned up — name conflict on new creation.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First LoadBalancer: No cloud provider integration — need MetalLB for on-prem.
  2. kubeadm without --cloud-provider flag: Cloud provider not configured.
  3. Private cluster: Nodes in private subnets — can't create internet-facing LB.
  4. Wrong service.beta.kubernetes.io annotations for cloud provider version.
  5. No external IP pool: MetalLB not configured with IP address range.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl describe svc <name> | grep -A10 Events. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep cloud-controller.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. For cloud: verify cloud-controller-manager is running
2. For bare metal: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/main/config/manifests/metallb-native.yaml
3. Configure MetalLB IP pool or verify cloud IAM permissions
4. Check Events in kubectl describe svc for exact error
5. Alternative: use NodePort + external LB (nginx/haproxy)

💡 Personal Advice: LoadBalancer <pending> on bare metal = you need MetalLB. On cloud = cloud-controller-manager issue or IAM permissions. On CKA: the exam environment is self-contained — you likely won't have cloud LBs. Know how to use NodePort as an alternative and understand that MetalLB provides LoadBalancer services on bare metal.
SN4
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN4
kube-proxy Not Running — No Service Routing

🔍 Symptom: All Services return connection refused. iptables -t nat -L shows no KUBE-SERVICES chain. kube-proxy DaemonSet pods not running on nodes.

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
NAME          READY   STATUS
❌ (empty or CrashLoopBackOff)

$ iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES
❌ iptables: No chain/target/match by that name
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. kube-proxy DaemonSet not running: kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy.
  2. kube-proxy CrashLoopBackOff: ConfigMap changed, invalid config, or missing conntrack module.
  3. Node taint blocks kube-proxy pod: DaemonSet doesn't tolerate control-plane taint.
  4. kube-proxy config file corrupted: /var/lib/kube-proxy/config.conf invalid.
  5. Container runtime not available: Node where kube-proxy scheduled has broken CRI.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI plugin not ready on node: kube-proxy waits for CNI before starting.
  2. kube-proxy --proxy-mode mismatch: Configured for IPVS but ip_vs module not loaded.
  3. kube-proxy hostNetwork: true pod can't start due to port conflict with host process.
  4. Kubernetes API server unreachable from node: kube-proxy can't watch Services/Endpoints.
  5. Disk full on node: kube-proxy can't write config files or iptables rules.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First cluster: kube-proxy deployed by kubeadm as DaemonSet — must be running on all nodes.
  2. kube-proxy uses hostNetwork: port 10249 (metrics) and 10256 (health) must be free.
  3. New node added: kube-proxy DaemonSet automatically schedules but may fail on tainted node.
  4. Wrong kubeconfig: kube-proxy can't authenticate to API server.
  5. kube-proxy running but iptables rules not updated: Check kube-proxy --write-config-to.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get ds -n kube-system kube-proxy. kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy. iptables -t nat -L KUBE-SERVICES on node.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
2. Check logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy
3. Restart: kubectl rollout restart ds kube-proxy -n kube-system
4. On node: lsmod | grep ip_vs if using IPVS
5. Recreate: kubectl delete pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy

💡 Personal Advice: kube-proxy is essential — without it, Services don't work. It runs as a DaemonSet on EVERY node, writing iptables/IPVS rules. If ALL Services fail, check kube-proxy first. On CKA: you may see a node where Services don't work — check if kube-proxy pod is running on that specific node.
SN5
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN5
Session Affinity Broken — Sticky Sessions Not Working

🔍 Symptom: Service configured with sessionAffinity: ClientIP but requests from same client go to different pods. Session state lost. Application session management broken.

$ kubectl get svc web-svc -o yaml | grep -A3 sessionAffinity
sessionAffinity: ClientIP
sessionAffinityConfig:
  clientIP:
    timeoutSeconds: 10800
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Client behind NAT/proxy: Source IP changes — different IP = different session affinity.
  2. kube-proxy in IPVS mode with wrong scheduler: IPVS persistence needs specific configuration.
  3. sessionAffinity timeout too short: Default 10800s (3h) may be too long or too short for your app.
  4. Multiple clients sharing same source IP (corporate NAT): All traffic goes to SAME pod — overload.
  5. Ingress in front of Service: Ingress strips original client IP — Service sees Ingress IP.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. LoadBalancer with externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster — source NAT hides real client IP.
  2. NodePort accessed via different nodes: Each node has independent session affinity tables.
  3. kube-proxy restart: Session affinity table lost on kube-proxy restart.
  4. Multiple Services targeting same pods: Different session tracking tables per Service.
  5. IPv6 to IPv4 NAT: Source IP translation breaks session affinity.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. New Service without sessionAffinity: Default is None (random load balancing).
  2. Sticky sessions at wrong layer: Using L4 (ClientIP) when L7 (cookie-based) needed.
  3. Ingress Controller session affinity not configured: Ingress-level sticky sessions needed for HTTP.
  4. Service mesh sidecar: Istio/Linkerd proxy breaks ClientIP-based affinity.
  5. Cloud LB has its own session affinity: Conflicts with Kubernetes sessionAffinity.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep HOSTNAME — which pod served request. kubectl logs <pod> | grep <client-ip>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Use Ingress-level cookie-based affinity for HTTP workloads
2. Set externalTrafficPolicy: Local to preserve client IP
3. Check if client is behind NAT: kubectl exec <pod> -- echo $REMOTE_ADDR
4. For IPVS: configure persistence timeout in kube-proxy config
5. Consider application-level session management (Redis/JWT) instead of transport-level

💡 Personal Advice: sessionAffinity: ClientIP is a blunt instrument — it only works when the client IP is stable. For modern apps behind load balancers, proxies, and NAT, ClientIP is unreliable. Use application-level sessions (Redis, JWT tokens) or Ingress-level cookie-based affinity. On CKA: understand sessionAffinity exists but know its limitations — never rely on it for production stateful apps.

📌 SN6–SN10: DNS & CoreDNS Failures

SN6
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN6
CoreDNS Pods CrashLoopBackOff — DNS Down Cluster-Wide

🔍 Symptom: All CoreDNS pods crashing, kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns shows CrashLoopBackOff. No DNS resolution anywhere.

$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
NAME                      READY   STATUS
❌ coredns-7d8f9-abc        0/1     CrashLoopBackOff

$ kubectl logs -n kube-system coredns-7d8f9-abc
❌ plugin/loop: Loop (127.0.0.1:xxxxx -> 127.0.0.1:53) detected, shutting down
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Loop detection triggered: CoreDNS detects forwarding loop (upstream DNS = CoreDNS itself). Check Corefile config.
  2. CoreDNS ConfigMap corrupted: Invalid Corefile syntax. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml.
  3. Upstream DNS unreachable: forward . /etc/resolv.conf — node's DNS not working.
  4. CoreDNS OOMKilled: Memory limit too low for cluster size. 10K+ services = more memory needed.
  5. Port 53 conflict: Node-local DNS cache or systemd-resolved using port 53.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Node DNS override: systemd-resolved stub listener on 127.0.0.53 confusing CoreDNS.
  2. CoreDNS using wrong cluster domain: kubernetes cluster.local vs custom domain.
  3. CoreDNS plugin conflict: Both kubernetes and forward plugins for same zone.
  4. Prometheus metrics endpoint causing high memory: Large cluster with scrape enabled.
  5. CoreDNS cache poisoning from upstream DNS returning bad responses.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First deployment: CoreDNS deployed by kubeadm with default ConfigMap — may need tuning.
  2. Node DNS misconfigured: /etc/resolv.conf on nodes has unreachable nameservers.
  3. CoreDNS with 1 replica only: No redundancy. Any failure = DNS down.
  4. CoreDNS anti-affinity not configured: All replicas on same node — single point of failure.
  5. Cluster domain mismatch: kubelet --cluster-domain differs from CoreDNS kubernetes plugin config.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns --tail=50. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Check logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
2. Fix loop: in Corefile, change forward . /etc/resolv.conf to specific upstream (8.8.8.8)
3. kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system and fix syntax errors
4. Increase replicas: kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=2
5. kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system

💡 Personal Advice: CoreDNS CrashLoopBackOff is usually a loop detection or ConfigMap error. The loop detection safety net kills CoreDNS to prevent infinite DNS loops. Fix: edit the ConfigMap and remove the loop by using proper upstream DNS. On CKA: you may need to fix a broken CoreDNS — check logs first, then ConfigMap.
SN7
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN7
Pod DNS Resolution Slow or Intermittent

🔍 Symptom: DNS resolution from pods takes 5+ seconds or sometimes fails. nslookup in pod works sometimes, fails others. CoreDNS overloaded or misconfigured.

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- time nslookup kubernetes.default
real    0m5.234s  ← 5 seconds! (should be <100ms)

$ kubectl top pod -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-dns
NAME                      CPU    MEMORY
❌ coredns-7d8f9-abc        500m   200Mi  ← High CPU!
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. CoreDNS overloaded: Too many DNS queries. Add replicas and enable caching.
  2. Network latency between pod and CoreDNS: Pod in different AZ/region from CoreDNS pod.
  3. DNS search domains too long: /etc/resolv.conf has many search domains — each tried sequentially.
  4. CoreDNS cache disabled: cache 30 missing from Corefile. Every query hits upstream.
  5. Upstream DNS slow: forward . /etc/resolv.conf pointing to slow corporate DNS.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. ndots:5 causing excessive DNS queries: Default ndots=5 makes every name tried with search domains.
  2. CoreDNS autopath plugin enabled: Cache miss on every query — always walks search path.
  3. Node-local DNS cache missing: Every DNS query goes to CoreDNS pod (network hop).
  4. IPv6 DNS queries timing out: Pod has IPv6 enabled but cluster has no IPv6 DNS.
  5. DNS over TCP retry after UDP failure: UDP packet loss causes 5s TCP fallback delay.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. Default CoreDNS config with 1 replica: Any load spike = slow DNS.
  2. No node-local-dns: Queries traverse overlay network to CoreDNS pod.
  3. Cluster with 100+ services: CoreDNS needs more resources at scale.
  4. ndots:5 (default) too high: Pod tries 5 search domain variations before absolute lookup.
  5. No DNS monitoring: Can't see query rate, latency, error rate trends.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- cat /etc/resolv.conf. kubectl exec <pod> -- time nslookup kubernetes.default.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Scale CoreDNS: kubectl scale deploy coredns -n kube-system --replicas=3
2. Enable cache: add cache 30 to Corefile
3. Reduce ndots: set dnsConfig: options: - name: ndots value: "2" in pod spec
4. Add node-local-dns: DaemonSet caching DNS on each node
5. Use specific upstream: forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4

💡 Personal Advice: DNS slowness is often ndots=5 + search domains + caching issues. The pod resolver tries 5 suffix combinations before using absolute name. Fix: reduce ndots to 2, enable CoreDNS cache, scale replicas. On CKA: you may see slow DNS — check /etc/resolv.conf for excessive search domains and adjust ndots.
SN8
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN8
External DNS Resolution Fails — Can't Reach Internet

🔍 Symptom: Pods can resolve internal Services but external names (google.com, github.com) fail. forward plugin in CoreDNS misconfigured or node DNS broken.

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup google.com
❌ ;; connection timed out; no servers could be reached

$ kubectl exec test-pod -- nslookup kubernetes.default
✅ Server: 10.96.0.10  Address: 10.96.0.10#53  Name: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Upstream DNS unreachable: CoreDNS forward block points to bad DNS. Check Corefile.
  2. Node /etc/resolv.conf has wrong DNS: CoreDNS inherits node's upstream DNS by default.
  3. Firewall blocking outbound DNS (UDP 53): CoreDNS can't reach external DNS servers.
  4. Corporate DNS requires specific search domains: Pod search domains don't include corporate domain.
  5. DNS policy on pod: dnsPolicy: None with custom DNS ignoring CoreDNS.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. NetworkPolicy blocks CoreDNS egress to external DNS: Allow UDP 53 to upstream DNS IPs.
  2. Proxy requiring authentication: DNS queries blocked by transparent proxy.
  3. Upstream DNS rate limiting: Too many queries from cluster — external DNS throttling.
  4. DNS64/NAT64 misconfigured: IPv6-only cluster can't reach IPv4 DNS servers.
  5. Stub domain in Corefile: example.com:53 { forward . 10.0.0.1 } not working.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First cluster with no internet: Air-gapped — need internal DNS forwarding for external names.
  2. CoreDNS forward to node DNS by default: forward . /etc/resolv.conf — if node DNS broken, all external fails.
  3. No upstream DNS configured in Corefile: forward . /etc/resolv.conf inherited from kubeadm defaults.
  4. Custom cluster domain: <domain> not resolving because CoreDNS doesn't forward unknown domains.
  5. Cloud DNS (Route 53) VPC resolver not accessible from pod network.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl exec <pod> -- nslookup google.com. kubectl get cm coredns -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -A5 forward.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Fix Corefile: forward . 8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4 instead of /etc/resolv.conf
2. Verify node DNS: nslookup google.com from node — if fails, fix node DNS
3. Allow UDP 53 egress in NetworkPolicy
4. kubectl rollout restart deploy coredns -n kube-system
5. For air-gapped: configure internal DNS forwarder for allowed external domains

💡 Personal Advice: Kubernetes DNS (internal) works but external fails = CoreDNS forward plugin issue. CoreDNS uses node's /etc/resolv.conf as upstream by default — if the node's DNS is broken, external resolution fails cluster-wide. On CKA: you may need to configure CoreDNS upstream DNS servers. Know: kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system and the forward . block.

📌 SN11–SN15: Network Policy Troubleshooting

SN11
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN11
NetworkPolicy Applied — Pods Can't Communicate

🔍 Symptom: After applying NetworkPolicy, pods can't reach each other. Policy is too restrictive or default-deny blocks legitimate traffic. Applications broken.

$ kubectl get networkpolicy -A
NAMESPACE  NAME        POD-SELECTOR
default    deny-all    {}  ← Blocks everything!

$ kubectl exec web-pod -- curl api-svc:8080
❌ curl: (28) Connection timed out after 3000ms
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. Default-deny applied without allow rules: podSelector: {} and empty ingress/egress = blocks ALL traffic.
  2. podSelector too broad: Selects ALL pods when you meant only specific pods.
  3. Missing allow rule for DNS: UDP 53 not allowed — pods can't resolve Service names.
  4. namespaceSelector mismatch: Rule allows "team: dev" but namespace has label "team: development".
  5. egress rules block responses: TCP needs bidirectional rules — egress must allow return traffic.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. CNI plugin doesn't support NetworkPolicy: Flannel by itself silently ignores all NetworkPolicies.
  2. ipBlock CIDR too narrow: Allowed range doesn't include the actual source IP of the traffic.
  3. NetworkPolicy ordering: Multiple policies on same pod — UNION of allows. One deny-all blocks nothing if any allow exists.
  4. Pod needs to talk to itself (localhost): Not covered by NetworkPolicy — always allowed.
  5. kubelet health checks blocked: Node IP not in allowed ipBlocks — probes fail.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First NetworkPolicy: Default behavior is ALLOW ALL. NP is opt-in restriction.
  2. Created default-deny first without any allow rules — everything breaks immediately.
  3. CNI not tested with NP: New cluster with Flannel — NetworkPolicy YAML applies but silently ignored.
  4. Namespace label dance: NP selects by namespace labels — labels must exist on namespace objects.
  5. NetworkPolicy is namespaced: Rules apply only within the NP's namespace.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get networkpolicy -A. kubectl describe networkpolicy <name> -n <ns>. kubectl exec <pod> -- curl <svc>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Start with allow rule, then add restrictions: don't start with deny-all
2. Always allow DNS: UDP 53 from all pods
3. Allow kubelet probes: add node CIDR to ipBlock
4. Test: kubectl run test --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -O- <svc>
5. Verify CNI supports NP: Calico/Cilium/Weave = yes, Flannel alone = no

💡 Personal Advice: NetworkPolicy is a scalpel — default-deny first = broken cluster. Always start with allow rules, then add a default-deny LAST (after verifying allows work). The #1 mistake: applying deny-all and wondering why everything broke. Also: Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy. On CKA: you'll create policies — always allow DNS first (UDP 53).
SN15
🔧 CATEGORY SN — Issue SN15
Ingress Controller Not Picking Up Ingress Resources

🔍 Symptom: Ingress YAML applied successfully but kubectl describe ingress shows no events. Ingress controller not running or ingressClassName mismatch.

$ kubectl get ingress
NAME        CLASS    HOSTS   ADDRESS   PORTS
my-ingress  nginx    app.com           80

$ kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress
❌ (empty — no Ingress controller running!)

$ curl http://<node-ip>
❌ curl: (7) Failed to connect
🔴5 Most Likely
  1. No Ingress controller installed: Ingress is just rules — need controller (nginx, traefik) to implement them.
  2. ingressClassName mismatch: Ingress specifies "nginx" but controller uses class "nginx-internal".
  3. Ingress controller pod not running: kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx.
  4. Wrong namespace: Ingress controller in namespace X but Ingress resource expects it in namespace Y.
  5. Ingress controller Service type wrong: NodePort used but firewall blocks the port.
🟡5 Less Likely
  1. Multiple Ingress controllers: Both trying to handle the same Ingress — conflict.
  2. Ingress controller using different API group: extensions/v1beta1 vs networking.k8s.io/v1.
  3. TLS Secret missing: Ingress references a Secret that doesn't exist — controller rejects the Ingress.
  4. Ingress controller health check failing: Pod not ready — not processing Ingress resources.
  5. RBAC: Ingress controller ServiceAccount doesn't have permission to watch Ingress resources.
🟣5 New Cluster
  1. First Ingress: Must install controller first, then create Ingress resources.
  2. kubeadm doesn't install Ingress controller: Must add manually (unlike cloud managed K8s).
  3. IngressClassName required in K8s 1.22+: Older Ingress resources without class ignored by controller.
  4. Default IngressClass not set: kubectl get ingressclass — must designate one as default.
  5. Controller installed in wrong namespace: Ingress controller expects Ingress resources in specific namespaces.
🔍 What to Look At: kubectl get pods -A | grep ingress. kubectl get ingressclass. kubectl describe ingress <name>.
🔧 How to Solve:

1. Install controller: kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/main/deploy/static/provider/cloud/deploy.yaml
2. Verify: kubectl get pods -n ingress-nginx
3. Set ingressClassName to match controller
4. Create TLS Secret if referenced in Ingress
5. Test: curl -H "Host: app.com" http://<controller-ip>

💡 Personal Advice: Ingress without controller = just YAML in etcd. Nothing happens until you install an Ingress controller. On CKA: you'll need to create an Ingress resource. Know that the controller must be installed FIRST. Also: IngressClassName is required in K8s 1.22+. Without it, the controller won't pick up the Ingress.

5Categories
RealCopy-Paste YAML

💾 Category 1: Storage Lab ScenariosS1-S10

🟢 anihpj/jobpost — Full-Stack Django + PostgreSQL Application

What is anihpj/jobpost? A Django-based job board application where employers post jobs and applicants apply. It consists of a Django web server, PostgreSQL database, and Redis cache. Each scenario deploys a part of this app with intentional bugs — your job is to find and fix them.

S1
🧪 SCENARIO S1 — Category 1: Storage PVC Debug

Deploy anihpj PostgreSQL — Fix PVC Stuck in Pending

The Problem: You deploy the anihpj/jobpost PostgreSQL database using a StatefulSet with a PersistentVolumeClaim. The pod stays Pending because the PVC won't bind — the StorageClass name is misspelled as "fast-ssd" but the actual StorageClass is named "fast-ssd-sc". Your job: find the mismatch and fix it so the database starts correctly.
1

📋 Deploy anihpj PostgreSQL (CONTAINS THE BUG)

Copy this YAML and apply it to your kubeadm cluster. The PVC storageClassName is intentionally wrong — "fast-ssd" instead of "fast-ssd-sc".

BASH — Create the StorageClass + Deploy PostgreSQL with bug 
# ============================================
# FILE STRUCTURE for anihpj/jobpost (S1):
# 
# anihpj/
# ├── 00-namespace.yaml             ← kubectl create ns anihpj
# ├── 01-storageclass.yaml          ← fast-ssd-sc (default, no-provisioner)
# ├── 02-persistentvolume.yaml      ← anihpj-db-pv (hostPath, 10Gi)
# ├── 03-postgres-pvc.yaml          ← PVC with BUG: storageClassName "fast-ssd"
# ├── 04-postgres-statefulset.yaml  ← StatefulSet with BUG in volumeClaimTemplates
# └── 05-postgres-service.yaml      ← ClusterIP Service (port 5432)
# ============================================

# 1. CREATE NAMESPACE
kubectl create namespace anihpj

# 2. CREATE THE STORAGECLASS (correct name: fast-ssd-sc)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd-sc
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
EOF

# 3. CREATE THE PV (static provisioning)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 10Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: fast-ssd-sc
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/anihpj-db
EOF

# 4. DEPLOY PVC + STATEFULSET (BUG: storageClassName: "fast-ssd")
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-data
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
  storageClassName: fast-ssd    # ❌ BUG! Should be "fast-ssd-sc"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceName: anihpj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
      storageClassName: fast-ssd  # ❌ BUG! Same typo here
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF

# The APP STORY:
# anihpj/jobpost is a Django job board app.
# Employers post jobs, applicants apply.
# PostgreSQL stores: users, jobs, applications.
# Redis caches: job listings, session data.
# Django serves: REST API at /api, admin at /admin
# (Django image built separately — not needed for this lab)
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj
✗2. Check PVC: kubectl get pvc -n anihpj → STATUS: Pending
✗3. Check pod events: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-db-0 → "persistentvolumeclaim not found" or "pod has unbound PVC"
✗4. The database pod cannot start — job board is DOWN!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Describe the PVC: kubectl describe pvc -n anihpj anihpj-db-data
→ Events: "storageclass.storage.k8s.io 'fast-ssd' not found"
2Check available StorageClasses: kubectl get sc
→ Only "fast-ssd-sc" exists (with (default) annotation)
3Check PVC storageClassName: kubectl get pvc -n anihpj -o yaml | grep storageClassName
→ storageClassName: fast-ssd (WRONG!)
4Compare: PVC says fast-ssd — StorageClass is fast-ssd-sc
5Root cause: Typo in storageClassName — "fast-ssd" instead of "fast-ssd-sc"
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod Pending → Check Events
②
PVC not binding → Check SC name
③
kubectl get sc → "fast-ssd-sc" exists
④
PVC says "fast-ssd" → MISMATCH!
⑤
Fix PVC → Pod starts → DB ready

Tenet: When a PVC stays Pending, the #1 cause is a StorageClass name mismatch. The StorageClass must exist with the EXACT name specified in the PVC. Even one character off = PVC stuck Pending forever. Always run kubectl get sc BEFORE writing PVC YAML. On the CKA exam, this is one of the most common "fix a broken deployment" scenarios.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-db-0 0/1 Pending 0 2m
$ kubectl describe pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj | tail -5 Events: Warning FailedScheduling pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims Warning FailedScheduling persistentvolumeclaim "db-data-anihpj-db-0" not found
$ kubectl describe pvc anihpj-db-data -n anihpj | grep -A5 Events Events: Warning ProvisioningFailed storageclass.storage.k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found
$ kubectl get sc NAME PROVISIONER RECLAIMPOLICY VOLUMEBINDINGMODE fast-ssd-sc (default) kubernetes.io/no-provisioner Retain WaitForFirstConsumer
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY STORAGECLASS anihpj-db-data Bound anihpj-db-pv 10Gi fast-ssd-sc db-data-anihpj-db-0 Bound anihpj-db-pv 10Gi fast-ssd-sc
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE anihpj-db-0 1/1 Running 0 30s
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-db-0 -- psql -U anihpj -d jobpost -c "SELECT 1;" ?column? ---------- 1 (1 row) ✅ Database is operational!
🔧
BASH — Delete and recreate PVC with correct StorageClass 
# Step 1: Delete the broken StatefulSet + PVC
kubectl delete statefulset anihpj-db -n anihpj
kubectl delete pvc anihpj-db-data -n anihpj
kubectl delete pvc db-data-anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj 2>/dev/null

# Step 2: Recreate the PVC with CORRECT StorageClass
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-data
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
  storageClassName: fast-ssd-sc    # ✅ FIXED! Matches StorageClass name
EOF

# Step 3: Recreate StatefulSet with correct storageClassName
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceName: anihpj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
      storageClassName: fast-ssd-sc  # ✅ FIXED!
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    app: anihpj-db
  ports:
  - port: 5432
    targetPort: 5432
EOF

# Step 4: Wait for pod to be Ready
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj --timeout=120s
✓

✅ Verify — Database Is Running

After the fix, the PVC binds to the PV with StorageClass fast-ssd-sc. The StatefulSet creates the pod, PostgreSQL initializes, and the job board database is ready. kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows anihpj-db-0 Running 1/1 and kubectl get pvc -n anihpj shows STATUS: Bound.

🧹
BASH — copy & paste to clean up 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv anihpj-db-pv

# Delete the StorageClass
kubectl delete sc fast-ssd-sc

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv,sc -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S2
🧪 SCENARIO S2 — Category 1: Storage AccessMode Debug

RWO vs RWX — Two anihpj API Pods, One Volume

The Problem: You deploy two replicas of the anihpj-api pod. Both need to share a single PersistentVolume for session data. One pod starts fine. The second pod stays Pending because the PV uses ReadWriteOnce (RWO) — only one node can mount it at a time. Your job: understand accessModes and fix it so both API pods can run simultaneously.
1

📋 Deploy anihpj API with Shared Volume (CONTAINS THE BUG)

The PV is created with RWO access. Two API replicas try to use it — only one will succeed.

BASH — Deploy PV + PVC + Deployment with bug 
# anihpj/
# ├── 01-persistentvolume.yaml   ← PV with RWO (BUG!)
# ├── 02-persistentvolumeclaim.yaml
# └── 03-api-deployment.yaml     ← 2 replicas sharing one PVC
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: anihpj-session-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce    # ❌ BUG! RWO = one node only
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/anihpj-sessions
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-session-pvc
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 2    # ❌ Only 1 will run with RWO!
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: nginx:alpine
        volumeMounts:
        - name: session-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/sessions
      volumes:
      - name: session-data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: anihpj-session-pvc
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe the Error — Spot What's Broken

✗1. Check pods: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
✗2. One Running, one Pending — only 1/2 replicas up
✗3. Describe pending pod → "Multi-Attach error for volume"
✗4. API single-point-of-failure — job board DOWN risk!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Root Cause

1Check PV accessModes: kubectl get pv anihpj-session-pv
→ ReadWriteOnce — single node only!
2Check pod nodes: kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide
→ Pods on different nodes — RWO blocks 2nd mount!
3Check events: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj <pending-pod>
→ Multi-Attach error — volume already attached to node-1
4Root cause: RWO allows only ONE node to mount. Two pods on different nodes = 2nd pod blocked. Need ReadWriteMany (RWX) or pod affinity.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
2 replicas → Pod Pending
②
Multi-Attach error → Check PV
③
RWO found → 1 node only
④
Need RWX or podAffinity
⑤
Fix → Both pods Running

Tenet: AccessModes are non-negotiable. RWO = 1 node, RWX = many nodes. For shared data across replicas, use RWX (NFS/EFS/GlusterFS). On CKA: when two pods need one volume, check accessModes first.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide NAME READY STATUS NODE anihpj-api-abc 1/1 Running node-1 anihpj-api-xyz 0/1 Pending <none>
$ kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-api-xyz | tail -5 Events: Warning FailedAttachVolume Multi-Attach error for volume "anihpj-session-pv" Warning FailedMount Unable to attach or mount volumes
$ kubectl get pv anihpj-session-pv -o yaml | grep -A3 accessModes accessModes: - ReadWriteOnce ← BUG! Single-node only
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o wide NAME READY STATUS NODE anihpj-api-abc 1/1 Running node-1 anihpj-api-xyz 1/1 Running node-1
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-api-abc -- wget -qO- http://localhost:80 <!DOCTYPE html> <html> <head><title>Welcome to nginx!</title></head> <body> <h1>Welcome to nginx!</h1> <p>If you see this page, the nginx web server is successfully installed.</p> </body> </html> ✅ Both API pods serving!
🔧
BASH — Fix options 
# Option A: Scale to 1 (RWO works with single pod)
kubectl scale deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj --replicas=1

# Option B: Pod affinity — both pods on same node
kubectl patch deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"affinity":{"podAffinity":{"requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution":[{"labelSelector":{"matchLabels":{"app":"anihpj-api"}},"topologyKey":"kubernetes.io/hostname"}]}}}}}}'
kubectl scale deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj --replicas=2

# Option C (production): Use EFS/NFS with RWX accessMode
✓

✅ Verify — Both Pods Running

With podAffinity or 1 replica: kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows all pods Running. The API is healthy. Long-term fix: use RWX storage (NFS/EFS).

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv anihpj-session-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S3
🧪 SCENARIO S3 — Category 1: Storage PVC Expansion

Expand PVC for Growing jobpost Database

The Problem: The anihpj/jobpost PostgreSQL database is running low on disk (5Gi PVC almost full). You patch the PVC from 5Gi to 20Gi. The patch succeeds but the PVC stays at 5Gi. The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: false. Your job: enable expansion and grow the database volume.
1

📋 Deploy PostgreSQL with Small PVC (CONTAINS THE BUG)

StorageClass created with allowVolumeExpansion: false. PVC starts at 5Gi.

BASH — SC + PV + PVC + StatefulSet 
# anihpj/
# ├── 01-storageclass.yaml    ← allowVolumeExpansion: false (BUG!)
# ├── 02-persistentvolume.yaml
# ├── 03-postgres-pvc.yaml    ← 5Gi too small
# └── 04-postgres-sts.yaml
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: expandable-sc
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner
allowVolumeExpansion: false    # ❌ BUG! Blocks PVC resize
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 20Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: expandable-sc
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/anihpj-db-s3
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-data
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
  storageClassName: expandable-sc
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceName: anihpj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15-alpine
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
        - name: POSTGRES_USER
          value: anihpj
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
        volumeMounts:
        - name: db-data
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: db-data
    spec:
      accessModes:
      - ReadWriteOnce
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 5Gi
      storageClassName: expandable-sc
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Try to Expand, It Fails

✗1. Try resize: kubectl patch pvc anihpj-db-data -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'
✗2. Check PVC: kubectl get pvc -n anihpj → CAPACITY still 5Gi
✗3. Describe PVC: "FileSystemResizePending" — not progressing
✗4. Database filling up — jobpost may crash!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Why Won't the PVC Expand?

1Check SC: kubectl get sc expandable-sc -o yaml | grep allowVolumeExpansion
→ allowVolumeExpansion: false — BLOCKED!
2Check PVC conditions: kubectl get pvc -n anihpj -o yaml
→ FileSystemResizePending but SC blocks it
3Root cause: StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: false. PVC resize request is recorded but never executed. Must enable expansion on SC first.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
PVC patch → Size unchanged
②
Check SC → allowVolumeExpansion: false
③
Enable expansion → Restart pod
④
PVC resized → DB has room

Tenet: PVC expansion needs: (1) SC allowVolumeExpansion:true, (2) PVC spec updated, (3) Pod restarted. On CKA: always check kubectl get sc -o yaml | grep allowVolumeExpansion when resize fails.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl patch pvc anihpj-db-data -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}' persistentvolumeclaim/anihpj-db-data patched
$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj NAME STATUS CAPACITY anihpj-db-data Bound 5Gi ← STILL 5Gi!
$ kubectl get sc expandable-sc -o yaml | grep allow allowVolumeExpansion: false ← BLOCKED!
$ kubectl describe pvc -n anihpj anihpj-db-data | grep -A3 Conditions Conditions: Type: FileSystemResizePending Status: True
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj NAME STATUS CAPACITY anihpj-db-data Bound 20Gi ← EXPANDED!
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data Filesystem Size Used Avail Use% Mounted on /dev/sdb 20G 1.2G 19G 6% /var/lib/postgresql/data ✅
🔧
BASH — Enable expansion + patch PVC + restart pod 
# Step 1: Enable volume expansion
kubectl patch sc expandable-sc -p '{"allowVolumeExpansion": true}'

# Step 2: Patch PVC to 20Gi
kubectl patch pvc anihpj-db-data -n anihpj -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"20Gi"}}}}'

# Step 3: Restart pod to trigger filesystem resize
kubectl delete pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj

# Step 4: Wait and verify
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj --timeout=120s
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data
✓

✅ Verify — PVC Expanded to 20Gi

kubectl get pvc -n anihpj shows CAPACITY: 20Gi. The filesystem inside the pod has 20Gi usable. jobpost can grow for months.

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv anihpj-db-pv

# Delete the StorageClass
kubectl delete sc expandable-sc

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv,sc -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S4
🧪 SCENARIO S4 — Category 1: Storage ConfigMap Volume

ConfigMap as Volume — Mount nginx Config into anihpj-web

The Problem: You mount a custom nginx config into the anihpj-web pod via ConfigMap as a volume, using subPath. Later you update the ConfigMap — but the pod still serves the OLD config. subPath prevents automatic ConfigMap updates from reaching the mounted file. Your job: understand subPath behavior and fix the config delivery.
1

📋 Deploy ConfigMap + Pod with subPath (CONTAINS THE BUG)

ConfigMap mounted via subPath — changes to ConfigMap won't update the mounted file!

BASH — ConfigMap + Pod with subPath bug 
# anihpj/
# ├── 01-configmap.yaml       ← nginx config
# └── 02-web-pod.yaml         ← Pod mounting ConfigMap
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: nginx-config
  namespace: anihpj
data:
  default.conf: |
    server {
      listen 80;
      location / { return 200 "VERSION-1"; }
    }
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj, labels: {app: anihpj-web}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config-vol
      mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
      subPath: default.conf    # ❌ BUG! subPath blocks updates
  volumes:
  - name: config-vol
    configMap:
    name: nginx-config
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe — ConfigMap Updated, Pod Serves Old Config

✗1. Update ConfigMap: kubectl patch cm nginx-config -n anihpj --type merge -p '{"data":{"default.conf":"server { listen 80; location / { return 200 \"VERSION-2\"; } }"}}'
✗2. Wait 2 min (kubelet sync period) — check pod: kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost → Still "VERSION-1"!
✗3. ConfigMap updated — pod NOT reflecting changes!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Why Isn't the Config Refreshing?

1Check mount: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-web | grep -A5 Mounts
→ subPath: default.conf — prevents symlink updates!
2Check ConfigMap hash: kubectl get cm nginx-config -n anihpj -o yaml | head
→ ConfigMap IS updated — but pod can't see it
3Root cause: subPath mounts use bind-mount of a specific file. The kubelet does NOT update subPath mounts when the ConfigMap changes. Without subPath, the entire directory is a symlink that gets refreshed.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Update CM → Pod unchanged
②
Check mount → subPath used
③
subPath = no auto-update
④
Remove subPath or restart pod

Tenet: subPath mounts are static file bind-mounts. They do NOT receive ConfigMap updates. For auto-updating configs, mount the entire ConfigMap as a directory (no subPath). On CKA: if config updates aren't reflected in pods, check for subPath usage.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost VERSION-1
$ kubectl get cm nginx-config -n anihpj -o yaml | grep VERSION location / { return 200 "VERSION-2"; } ← ConfigMap IS updated!
$ kubectl describe pod -n anihpj anihpj-web | grep -A3 Mounts Mounts: /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf from config-vol (rw,path="default.conf") subPath: default.conf ← Blocks auto-refresh!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost VERSION-2 ✅ Config refreshed!
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-web -- cat /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf server { listen 80; location / { return 200 "VERSION-2"; } }
🔧
BASH — Fix options 
# Option A: Remove subPath (pod needs recreate)
kubectl delete pod anihpj-web -n anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj, labels: {app: anihpj-web}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx:alpine
    volumeMounts:
    - name: config-vol
      mountPath: /etc/nginx/conf.d    # ✅ No subPath — auto-updates work
  volumes:
  - name: config-vol
        configMap:
          name: nginx-config
EOF

# Option B: Trigger restart to pick up new ConfigMap
kubectl rollout restart deployment anihpj-web-deploy -n anihpj 2>/dev/null || kubectl delete pod anihpj-web -n anihpj

# Option C: Use checksum annotation to force restart on CM change
kubectl patch deployment anihpj-web -n anihpj --patch "
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: $(kubectl get cm nginx-config -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data}' | sha256sum)"
✓

✅ Verify — Config Refreshes Automatically

After removing subPath, kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-web -- wget -qO- http://localhost shows VERSION-2. Future ConfigMap changes will propagate within ~1 min (kubelet sync period).

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything (ConfigMap included)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get cm,pods -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S5
🧪 SCENARIO S5 — Category 1: Storage emptyDir vs Persistent

emptyDir vs Persistent — Data After Pod Restart

The Problem: You deploy Redis for the jobpost cache using an emptyDir volume. Redis stores session data and cached job listings. The pod gets evicted or restarted — and all the cached data is GONE. emptyDir is ephemeral — data lives only as long as the pod. Your job: understand when to use emptyDir vs PersistentVolume and migrate Redis to durable storage.
1

📋 Deploy Redis with emptyDir (CONTAINS THE BUG)

Redis uses emptyDir — all data is lost on pod restart!

BASH — Redis Pod with emptyDir volume 
# anihpj/
# └── 01-redis-pod.yaml    ← emptyDir (BUG! data lost on restart)
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis
  namespace: anihpj, labels: {app: anihpj-redis}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:7-alpine
    ports:
        - containerPort: 6379
    volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: redis-data
    emptyDir: {}    # ❌ BUG! Ephemeral — data lost on restart
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector: {app: anihpj-redis}
  ports:
  - port: 6379
EOF

# Load test data into Redis
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli SET job-count 500
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli SET last-crawl "2025-06-04"
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Kill the Pod, Data Disappears

✗1. Verify data exists: kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count → "500"
✗2. Kill the pod: kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj
✗3. Pod restarts — check data: kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count → (nil) — DATA GONE!
✗4. Cached job listings, session data — ALL LOST!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Why Is the Data Gone?

1Check volume type: kubectl get pod -n anihpj anihpj-redis -o yaml | grep -A2 emptyDir
→ emptyDir: {} — no backing storage!
2Understand emptyDir: emptyDir is tied to the pod's lifecycle. It's created when the pod starts on a node and destroyed when the pod is removed.
3Root cause: emptyDir is ephemeral storage. When the pod restarts (even on same node), a new emptyDir is created — all previous data is lost. For databases/caches, use PersistentVolume instead.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Data written to /data
②
Pod deleted → emptyDir destroyed
③
New pod → new emptyDir
④
Data gone → Use PVC instead

Tenet: emptyDir = scratch space, caching, temp files. PersistentVolume = databases, stateful apps. On CKA: if asked to preserve data across pod restarts, NEVER use emptyDir. Always use PVC+PV.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli SET job-count 500 OK
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count "500"
$ kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj pod "anihpj-redis" deleted
$ sleep 3 && kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count (nil) ← DATA GONE!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count "500"
$ kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj && sleep 5 && kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count "500" ✅ Data survived pod restart!
🔧
BASH — PVC + PV for Redis 
# Step 1: Create PV + PVC
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/anihpj-redis
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis-pvc
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 2Gi
EOF

# Step 2: Recreate Redis pod with PVC
kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis
  namespace: anihpj, labels: {app: anihpj-redis}
spec:
  containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:7-alpine
    volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: redis-data
    persistentVolumeClaim: {claimName: anihpj-redis-pvc}    # ✅ Durable!
EOF

# Step 3: Test persistence
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli SET job-count 500
kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj
sleep 5
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET job-count    # Should return "500"!
✓

✅ Verify — Data Survives Pod Restart

After migrating to PVC: delete the Redis pod, wait for recreation, run redis-cli GET job-count → returns "500". Data persists because the PVC outlives the pod. jobpost cache is now durable.

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv anihpj-redis-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S6
🧪 SCENARIO S6 — Category 1: Storage Secret Injection

Secret as Environment Variable — Database Password for anihpj-api

The Problem: The anihpj-api Deployment references a Secret named anihpj-db-credentials for the PostgreSQL password via secretKeyRef. But the Secret was never created. The API pod starts but can't connect to the database — it crashes with password authentication failed because the env var is empty. Your job: create the Secret correctly and verify the API connects.
1

📋 Deploy API referencing non-existent Secret (CONTAINS THE BUG)

The Deployment references anihpj-db-credentials Secret — but it doesn't exist!

BASH — Deploy API pod referencing missing Secret 
# anihpj/
# ├── 01-namespace.yaml
# └── 02-api-deployment.yaml  ← References missing Secret
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-api
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: busybox:1.36
        command: ["sh","-c","echo DB_PASS=$DB_PASSWORD; sleep 3600"]
        env:
        - name: DB_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: anihpj-db-credentials    # ❌ BUG! Secret doesn't exist
              key: password
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pod Can't Access Database

✗1. Check pod status: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → Running (but app fails)
✗2. Check logs: kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api → "DB_PASS=" (empty!)
✗3. Check events: kubectl get events -n anihpj → "MountVolume.SetUp failed for secret not found"
✗4. API can't authenticate to PostgreSQL — jobpost DOWN!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Find the Missing Secret

1Check if Secret exists: kubectl get secrets -n anihpj
→ No "anihpj-db-credentials" found!
2Check Deployment env ref: kubectl get deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj -o yaml | grep -A5 secretKeyRef
→ References secret "anihpj-db-credentials" key "password"
3Root cause: Secret was never created. The Deployment references a non-existent Secret. Env var DB_PASSWORD is empty → API can't authenticate.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
App crash → Check logs
②
Empty env var → Check Secret ref
③
Secret missing → Create it
④
API connects → App working

Tenet: Secrets must exist BEFORE pods that reference them. If a pod references a non-existent Secret via secretKeyRef, the container starts but the env var is empty. On CKA: always verify Secrets exist with kubectl get secrets -n <ns> before deploying workloads.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj No resources found in anihpj namespace.
$ kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api DB_PASS= ← EMPTY! Secret doesn't exist
$ kubectl get events -n anihpj | grep -i secret Warning FailedMount MountVolume.SetUp failed for volume "db-credentials"
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get secrets -n anihpj NAME TYPE DATA anihpj-db-credentials Opaque 2
$ kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api DB_PASS=secret123 ✅ Secret injected!
🔧
BASH — Create Secret + restart Deployment 
# Step 1: Create the Secret (base64 encode the password)
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-db-credentials   --from-literal=password=secret123   --from-literal=username=anihpj   -n anihpj

# Step 2: Verify Secret
kubectl get secret anihpj-db-credentials -n anihpj
kubectl get secret anihpj-db-credentials -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

# Step 3: Restart Deployment to pick up Secret
kubectl rollout restart deploy anihpj-api -n anihpj

# Step 4: Verify env var is now set
kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api
# Should show: DB_PASS=secret123
✓

✅ Verify — Secret Injected Correctly

kubectl logs -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-api shows DB_PASS=secret123. The API can now authenticate to PostgreSQL. On CKA: use kubectl create secret generic for quick Secret creation.

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything (Secret included)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get secrets,deploy,pods -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S7
🧪 SCENARIO S7 — Category 1: Storage CSI Driver

CSI Driver Missing — EBS Provisioning Fails for anihpj-db

The Problem: You configure a StorageClass using the ebs.csi.aws.com provisioner for dynamic PVC provisioning. When you create the PVC for the jobpost database, it stays Pending forever. The AWS EBS CSI driver is not installed on the cluster. Your job: diagnose the CSI driver issue and understand CSI architecture.
1

📋 Deploy StorageClass + PVC referencing CSI (CONTAINS THE BUG)

The StorageClass uses ebs.csi.aws.com — but the CSI driver isn't installed!

BASH — SC + PVC with missing CSI driver 
# anihpj/
# ├── 01-storageclass.yaml    ← ebs.csi.aws.com (BUG!)
# └── 02-postgres-pvc.yaml
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: ebs-sc
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com    # ❌ BUG! CSI driver not installed
parameters:
    type: gp3
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-data
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
  storageClassName: ebs-sc
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe — PVC Stuck Pending Forever

✗1. Check PVC: kubectl get pvc -n anihpj → STATUS: Pending
✗2. Describe PVC: kubectl describe pvc -n anihpj anihpj-db-data → "waiting for a volume to be created"
✗3. Check provisioner events: No PV being created — provisioner not responding
🔍

🔍 Debug — Why Isn't the PVC Being Provisioned?

1Check SC provisioner: kubectl get sc ebs-sc -o yaml | grep provisioner
→ ebs.csi.aws.com — AWS EBS CSI driver
2Check CSI drivers: kubectl get csidrivers
→ ebs.csi.aws.com NOT listed!
3Check CSI pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep ebs
→ No matching pods — driver not installed!
4Root cause: The EBS CSI driver is not installed on the cluster. Without the driver, the external-provisioner can't create EBS volumes. PVC stays Pending forever.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
PVC Pending → Check provisioner
②
CSI driver not in csidrivers list
③
No CSI pods in kube-system
④
Install driver → PVC Bound

Tenet: CSI (Container Storage Interface) drivers must be installed before StorageClasses that reference them. Check with kubectl get csidrivers. On CKA: if PVC is stuck Pending with a cloud provisioner, verify the CSI driver is running.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY anihpj-db-data Pending ← Stuck!
$ kubectl describe pvc -n anihpj anihpj-db-data | tail -3 Events: Warning ProvisioningFailed failed to provision volume with StorageClass "ebs-sc"
$ kubectl get csidrivers No resources found ← CSI driver not installed!
$ kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep ebs (no results) ← No EBS CSI driver pods
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pvc -n anihpj NAME STATUS VOLUME CAPACITY anihpj-db-data Bound anihpj-db-pv 20Gi ✅
$ kubectl get csidrivers NAME ATTACHREQUIRED PODINFOONMOUNT ebs.csi.aws.com true false ✅
🔧
BASH — Install EBS CSI driver OR switch to hostPath 
# Option A: Install AWS EBS CSI driver (on EKS)
kubectl apply -k "github.com/kubernetes-sigs/aws-ebs-csi-driver/deploy/kubernetes/overlays/stable/?ref=master"

# Option B: For CKA lab (no AWS) — use hostPath instead
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 20Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/anihpj-db
  storageClassName: ebs-sc
EOF

# Verify PVC binds
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
✓

✅ Verify — PVC Bound

After installing the CSI driver (or creating a manual PV), kubectl get pvc -n anihpj shows STATUS: Bound. The storage provisioning pipeline works end-to-end.

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the PV if created (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv anihpj-db-pv 2>/dev/null

# Delete the StorageClass
kubectl delete sc ebs-sc

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv,sc -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S8
🧪 SCENARIO S8 — Category 1: Storage Permissions

Volume Mount Permission Denied — fsGroup Fix

The Problem: The anihpj-db pod mounts a PersistentVolume, but PostgreSQL can't write to /var/lib/postgresql/data. Events show "permission denied". The container runs as user postgres (UID 999) but the volume is owned by root:root. Your job: use fsGroup in the pod's securityContext to fix permissions.
1

📋 Deploy PostgreSQL with HostPath Volume (CONTAINS THE BUG)

The volume is owned by root, but postgres runs as UID 999 — permission denied!

BASH — Pod with missing fsGroup 
# anihpj/
# ├── 01-persistentvolume.yaml
# └── 02-postgres-pod.yaml     ← Missing fsGroup!
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pg-data-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 5Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/data/pg-s8
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pg-data-pvc
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 5Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: postgres
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
    - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
    volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumes:
      - name: pgdata
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pg-data-pvc
  # ❌ BUG! No securityContext.fsGroup — volume owned by root
EOF
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pod CrashLoops with Permission Denied

✗1. Check pod: kubectl get pods -n anihpj → CrashLoopBackOff
✗2. Check logs: kubectl logs -n anihpj anihpj-db → "Permission denied" on /var/lib/postgresql/data
✗3. DB can't initialize — jobpost has no database!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Who Owns the Volume?

1Check volume permissions on node: ls -la /mnt/data/pg-s8 (if accessible)
→ drwxr-xr-x root:root — postgres can't write!
2Check container user: PostgreSQL runs as postgres (UID 999) inside container
3Root cause: No fsGroup set. The hostPath volume is owned by root:root, but postgres (UID 999) needs write access. Use securityContext.fsGroup to change volume ownership.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
CrashLoop → Check logs
②
Permission denied → Check ownership
③
Volume owned by root → fsGroup needed
④
Add fsGroup → Pod starts

Tenet: securityContext.fsGroup changes the group ownership of volume files to the specified GID. For PostgreSQL (UID 999), set fsGroup: 999. On CKA: when you see "permission denied" on a volume, check fsGroup.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS anihpj-db 0/1 CrashLoopBackOff 5
$ kubectl logs -n anihpj anihpj-db initdb: error: could not access directory "/var/lib/postgresql/data": Permission denied
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-db -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql 2>/dev/null || echo "Can't exec - pod crashing" error: unable to upgrade connection: container not found ("postgres") # Note: Can't exec into CrashLoopBackOff pod — use debug pod instead
$ kubectl debug -n anihpj anihpj-db --image=busybox -it -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql/data 2>/dev/null || ssh node-1 ls -la /mnt/data/pg-s8 total 4 drwxr-xr-x 2 root root 4096 Jun 4 10:00 . drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Jun 4 10:00 .. ← Owner is root:root!
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl get pods -n anihpj NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS anihpj-db 1/1 Running 0 ✅
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-db -- ls -la /var/lib/postgresql/data total 132 drwxr-xr-x 19 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 . drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Jun 4 10:05 .. drwx------ 6 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 base drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 global drwx------ 2 postgres postgres 4096 Jun 4 10:05 pg_commit_ts ... ✅ fsGroup fixed ownership! postgres can write
🔧
BASH — Delete pod, recreate with fsGroup 
# Step 1: Delete the broken pod
kubectl delete pod anihpj-db -n anihpj

# Step 2: Recreate with fsGroup
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 999    # ✅ Fix! Changes volume group ownership to 999 (postgres)
  containers:
  - name: postgres
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    env:
        - name: POSTGRES_DB
          value: jobpost
    - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: secret123
    volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumes:
      - name: pgdata
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: pg-data-pvc
EOF

# Also works with runAsUser + fsGroup
# runAsUser: 999
# runAsGroup: 999
✓

✅ Verify — PostgreSQL Initializes Successfully

kubectl get pods -n anihpj shows Running 1/1. PostgreSQL can now write to the volume because fsGroup changed the group ownership to GID 999. The jobpost database is initialized.

🧹
BASH 
# Delete namespace — cascades everything inside
kubectl delete namespace anihpj

# Delete the PV (not namespaced)
kubectl delete pv pg-data-pv

# Verify cleanup
kubectl get all,pvc,pv -n anihpj 2>/dev/null
kubectl get ns anihpj 2>/dev/null
S9
🧪 SCENARIO S9 — Category 1: Storage hostPath

hostPath Volume — Pod Rescheduled, Data Lost

The Problem: The anihpj-redis pod uses a hostPath volume on node-1 to store cached data at /data/redis. The node fails and the pod is rescheduled to node-2. The pod starts but all cached data is GONE — hostPath data is tied to a specific node. Your job: understand hostPath limitations and migrate to a proper solution.
1

📋 Deploy Redis with hostPath on Node-1 (CONTAINS THE BUG)

hostPath ties data to a specific node — pod reschedule = data loss!

BASH — Redis with hostPath (node-specific) 
# anihpj/
# └── 01-redis-pod.yaml    ← hostPath (BUG! node-specific data)
kubectl create namespace anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  nodeName: node-1    # Pin to specific node
  containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:7-alpine
    volumeMounts:
        - name: redis-data
          mountPath: /data
  volumes:
  - name: redis-data
    hostPath:
      path: /data/redis    # ❌ BUG! Data only on node-1
      type: DirectoryOrCreate
EOF

# Load data
kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli SET sessions 1000
⚠

⚠️ Observe — Pod Moves, Data Disappears

✗1. Verify data: kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions → "1000"
✗2. Simulate node failure: kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj --force --grace-period=0
✗3. Pod rescheduled to node-2 — check data: kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions → (nil)
✗4. All user sessions LOST — jobpost users logged out!
🔍

🔍 Debug — Why Is Data Lost?

1Check volume type: kubectl get pod -n anihpj anihpj-redis -o yaml | grep -A3 hostPath
→ hostPath: /data/redis on node-1's filesystem
2Check new pod's node: kubectl get pod -n anihpj anihpj-redis -o wide
→ Now on node-2! Different host filesystem
3Root cause: hostPath stores data on the NODE's filesystem. When the pod moves to a different node, the new node doesn't have the data. hostPath is for node-level daemons, not for application data.
🧠 Diagnostic Tenet (Thought Process)
①
Pod on node-1 → Data on /data/redis
②
Pod deleted → Rescheduled to node-2
③
New /data/redis empty → Data lost
④
Use PVC — data follows pod

Tenet: hostPath is NOT for application data. It's for node-level agents (Fluentd, monitoring). Application data MUST use PersistentVolumes with network storage (NFS/EBS/EFS) so data survives node/pod changes. On CKA: if asked about data loss after pod reschedule, check if hostPath is used.

📟 Command Outputs — ERROR State (BEFORE fix)
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions "1000"
$ kubectl get pod -n anihpj anihpj-redis -o wide NAME NODE anihpj-redis node-1
$ kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj --force --grace-period=0 pod "anihpj-redis" force deleted
$ kubectl get pod -n anihpj anihpj-redis -o wide NAME NODE anihpj-redis node-2 ← Rescheduled!
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions (nil) ← DATA LOST! New node doesn't have /data/redis
📟 Command Outputs — AFTER Fix
$ kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions "1000"
$ kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj && sleep 5 && kubectl exec -n anihpj anihpj-redis -- redis-cli GET sessions pod "anihpj-redis" deleted pod/anihpj-redis condition met "1000" ✅ Data survived node change!
🔧
BASH — Replace hostPath with PVC 
# Step 1: Create PV (simulating NFS/EBS)
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: redis-data-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 2Gi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/shared/redis  # Would be NFS/EBS in production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: redis-data-pvc
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 2Gi
EOF

# Step 2: Recreate pod with PVC
kubectl delete pod anihpj-redis -n anihpj
cat << 'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-redis
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  containers:
  - name: redis
    image: redis:7-alpine
